utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, are you ready to proceed and continue with Dr. Gow, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before I do that, there has been a request from the Registry that we deal with the hard copy exhibits rather than the mechanical electronic process which we started with yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will have to repeat that for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have been requested by the Registry to deal with original hard copies of the exhibits rather than through the electronic means we started off with yesterday. We are in a position to do that, your Honours, but I only have one copy of each exhibit and I would, because I am dealing with it manually, be assisted at the Bar table by our case manager, Miss Sutherland, so that she can assist me with handling the hard copy exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What do you mean "deal with", in terms of the witness marking on the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have received a request that rather than -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I hear you; I just do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will just do it manually now, your Honours. I will tender the exhibit in hard copy. It will be handed to the witness in the usual way and marked in the usual way. The witness will deal with it in the usual way. Then when I ask the witness to explain something about the exhibit, we will use the video display.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might I have leave for Miss Sutherland to approach the Bar table?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. DR. JAMES GOW, recalled. Examined by MR. NIEMANN, continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you went into certain matters yesterday that led to the creation of the Yugoslav Federation which was subsequently to disintegrate in the 1990s. We had got to the point, I think, after World War II where you made mention of Tito. What role did Tito play in the federal system that was subsequently to be established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tito was the leader of the Communist movement leading the partisans and then which was installed in power after the Second World War. It adopted a federal form of governmen for the country. In part, this was a way of selling the idea of a new Yugoslavia to those who had been disaffected with the first Yugoslavia, but it must be stressed that, as far as the communists were concerned, they never, I would say, intended this system to have any real meaning. So, it was a federal in form, a federal constitution, which the Yugoslav communists had borrowed from the Soviet communists as a model, but one which did, nonetheless, make some concession to national questions within the territories of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with that, would you look, please, at a document that is now shown to you? Might this document be shown to the witness? (Handed). Dr. Gow, just looking at that, what I have shown to you, can you tell me what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first page is the cover page of a volume called "Yugoslavia Through Documents" edited by Snezana Trifunovska, and the remainder of the document are extracts from the Constitution of the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia as constituted on 31st January 1946.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where it was obtained from, that particular document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this form it was obtained by the Office of the Prosecutor from the publishers, Martinus Nijhoff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I tender the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Has that been given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it is the next number which is 18.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 18 being admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 18 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps the document might be marked, your Honour. After the document has been marked, might it be handed back to Dr. Gow, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you going to show Exhibit 18 on the monitor at some time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are not going to use the computer, your Honour, we will use the video.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The overhead projector? Very good. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, just going, in particular, to Articles 1 and 9 of that exhibit, and perhaps we can assist you. Miss Sutherland, could you display those Articles on the overhead projector?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Once we get all the technology together, then everything will go very smoothly if we can accomplish this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, dealing firstly with -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry. At the moment my screen is not wide enough to show it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps we are now having it ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is much larger. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, dealing firstly with Article 1, what, in your opinion, is the significance of this in terms of the provisions of Tito's postwar Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The significance of this first extract is that it focuses the formation of the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia, that it focuses the question of self-determination in the formation of the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia. Much of the mixture of historical, political and so forth evidence that I was giving yesterday was to identify factors leading to the formation of this federal state and to create the circumstances in which there is an understanding that that state was formed, at least formally, as a means of giving some concession to this principle of self-determination. You will see that it is formed on the basis of the right to self-determination, including the right of separation of those peoples who have come together living within those state forms. If you move to Article 2, you will see that the Federal People's Republic is composed of the various people's republics which are identified in Article 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving to Article 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 9 identifies clearly that in the complex system of sovereignties -- I would stress for the communists this was always more a formality than anything which had real meaning -- that sovereignty was clearly identified as resting with the People's Republics from the outset, as had been evolving during the Second World war in the AVNOJ system, the Anti-Fascist Council of National Liberation of Yugoslavia as the established government on territories that they liberated. Of course, you will also note (as is always the case in an arrangement of this kind) the sovereignty of the republic is in some sense offset by a different sovereignty of international personality of the Federal People's Republic as a whole. But I think, in principle, at a notional level, you would say that the sovereignty of the various -- the notional sovereignty of the various republics is transferred, some of those sovereign rights are transferred to the Federation in particular ways. This was certainly to be a significant question in 1991 in the process of dissolution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might the exhibit be returned to the Registry? Dr. Gow, you mentioned earlier that the constitutional model that we were just referring to had its origins from the Soviet Union. What was the relationship between the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia immediately following the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relationship between the two countries was both very close and increasingly very difficult. The Yugoslav communists sought to emulate the achievements of Stalin in the Soviet Union on the territories of Yugoslavia, but increasingly their attempts to do that brought them into conflict with Moscow, with Stalin, partly, I guess, because of a misunderstanding of the terms of what Stalinism was really supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after the break down of this relationship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1948 the relationship broke down. Yugoslavia was expelled from the communist bloc and this gave rise to the Yugoslav communists having to seek a different way, a different way for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was this different way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The label given to the different way was socialist self-management and the key, and again this was another formality laid upon other formalities, something which, I suspect, they never intended to have any real meaning, but one of the key features of that new formal mechanism was to say that there would be degrees of decentralisation. This was to have great significance for the evolution of the Yugoslav Federation thereafter, because increasingly people wanted, in practice, the kind of decentralisation which they were told according to the documents they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this postwar era, is it true to say that there was a centralising force and a corresponding decentralising force impact upon the Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be true. The communist party structures were essentially centralising. The communist party model is one of a strong degree of central control and central management, but this was always an intention with the evolution of the federal system with the idea of power being devolved. After this split in 1948, the Yugoslav communists had to justify to themselves and to their people why the split -- the causes of the split. They said the fault lay with the excessive centralisation of the Soviet Union; therefore, the solution to their problems was to have decentralisation. They still wanted to retain tight central control, but increasingly they were faced with some of their own members in parts of the country in the republic saying that things should be decentralised. It created a tension between centralism and decentralisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role, if any, did Tito play in this system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tito was essential for making that system work. Tito, as a result of leading the wartime movement, had enormous personal authority. Although there could be arguments between the different republican communist parties, all problems could be solved on the basis of Tito using his own personal authority. So, although it was a troubled system at various points through its 40 to 50 year history, while Tito was alive, Tito was always able to resolve problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the major developments in the constitutional evolution, if one might call it that, of Yugoslavia after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugoslav Federation faced a number of problems. In general, it tried to deal with those problems by creating new constitutional frameworks. It did this in 1954 and in 1963 and again in 1974. That process of evolution, particularly through the 1960s and into the 1970s, confirmed the transfer of real authority from the centre and from Belgrade which was the communist party headquarters for the whole of Yugoslavia which was both the federal capital and the capital of Serbia. It transferred power from Belgrade increasingly into the various republican capitals, into the party leaderships in those capitals, but also as a consequence of that into the state structures in those capitals as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask you to look at the document you are now shown. (Handed) Dr. Gow, what is the document that you have there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a copy of a translation of the 1974 Constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and in this present form is taken from Oceana Publications in New York.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you regard them as a reliable source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are a recognised and creditable publisher of legal documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is document 19, if your Honours please, and I tender that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 19 from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 19 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After the document has been marked, might we hand it back to the witness? (To the witness): Dr. Gow, with the assistance of Miss Sutherland, would you please go to section 8, page 25, of the document? Just looking at that, if it can be displayed -- I am not sure why it is not coming through, there we are -- particularly in relation to section 8. Dr. Gow, what, in your opinion, is the significance of these provisions in terms of the evolution of the decentralised confederation of which you were talking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This particular extract from the constitution identifies the central role which the communist party, which by this time had been renamed the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, played in the system. If you look to the second paragraph, if I may ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I will try to indicate. Just here, you will see that the guiding ideological, the guiding ideological and political action of the party as the prime mover and exponent of political activity is identified. This indicates clearly the way in which the communist party was intended to be the leading, the controlling, element within the federal structures, within the state structures as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, in what way is this significant in terms of what was ultimately to happen in terms of the disintegration of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is important in two ways. First, it is important for identifying the leading role of the communist party in the system as a whole, for exemplifying the way in which the communists understood that the communist party would be the key controlling element rather than the state structures. It is important at a second level because it is that leading role of the party as devolution occurred which consolidated the strength of the state structures in the various republics of the federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, perhaps that exhibit might be returned and if you look at this one that we are now showing to you? (Handed) Looking at that, what is this document I have just given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is a supplement by the editors of the same publication to which I have just made reference, that is the Oceana publication of the 1974 constitution. This is a supplement to the 1974 constitution issued in 1979 which indicates some of the important developments which occurred after the implementation of the constitution, matters which were pertinent to the implementation of that constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that exhibit, your Honour. It is document No. 20.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 20?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 20 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After it has been marked by the Registrar, I would ask you to go back to this document. If you could place page 1 on the screen, doctor? Perhaps that might be highlighted a little? It makes it slightly easier to read. If the document is pushed to the centre of the screen? Just having regard to that that appears there, Dr. Gow, what is the significance of this supplement in terms of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The supplement is significant because it identifies a number of ways in which the 1974 constitution was enabled to come into force, in particular on this, on the point I was just mentioning, I will draw your attention to the events of between May 27th and May 30th 1974, in particular, the meeting which new party statutes of the League of Communists were adopted and new party structures were established, thus enabling the party to take its leading role in establishing the constitutional structures. I draw your attention to the third line of the paragraph beginning "May 30", the paragraph which I have pointed to, in which the central committee membership was set at 165. This was based on party structures in each of the elements of the Federation, being 20 members from each of the republics and 15 from the two autonomous provinces (to which I made reference yesterday), a further 15 were taken from the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might that document be handed back to the Registry? Dr. Gow, speaking of these counter balancing forces of centralism and decentralism, how was the right of self-determination counter balanced by the forces of centralism in the Federation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The right to self-determination was embodied in the constitution in the preamble to the 1974 constitution, including the right of separation, but it was offset by Article 5 of the constitution to some extent which said that changes of this kind would have to be subject to the agreement of all elements in the Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was Article 5 of the 1974 constitution which is Exhibit 19?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case, and also the preamble to the same exhibit; if you wish, I would be able to indicate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, by reference to Exhibit 20 again that you had seen earlier -- perhaps that document might be shown to Dr. Gow, together with Exhibit 19 -- going firstly to Exhibit 19 and looking at Articles 1, 3 and 4 of that Exhibit, turning firstly to Article 1, could you tell me what, in your opinion, is the significance of this provision in terms of the sovereignty of the various republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The significance of Article 1 is identifying the Federation as a union of the various peoples brought together. It is significant in one sense because it uses the words "united nations", and the word "nation" in Serbo-Croat is "narod" which is also the word for "people", and there is a certain degree of ambiguity attached to this element in the constitution which is significant in some arguments which will come later. This clearly identifies, however, the position of the republics and this separate position of the two autonomous provinces within Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might look at Articles 3 and 4 of the same constitution which I would ask to be displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These two Articles extend the point that I was just making. If you see, Article 3 identifies the socialist republics, that is, the republic states of Serbia, Croatia, Montenegro, Macedonia, Slovenia and Bosnia and Herzegovina as being states based on the principle of sovereignty. Article 4 makes a distinction between those republics as states and the two autonomous provinces within Serbia which are not endowed with the quality of sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think now going back to Exhibit 20 at page 1 of that Exhibit and the introductory part, that also makes reference to this point, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you will excuse me, it is hard to read on the screen. The document is again -- I go back to the same point I was making before, and to emphasise that within these structures you had the communist party structures within the central committee of the Federation. The central committee was itself a federated body comprising membership from each of the various elements, the six republics and the two autonomous provinces, but also the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could those exhibits be returned, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I just also would indicate that just above that you will also see that the central federal body, the collective presidency -- sometimes now described as the State Council -- had a representative, eight representatives, one from each of the six republics, two, one each from the two autonomous provinces. This was consolidating the federal system and the representation of the elements within the federal system as constituting the Federation itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Might those two exhibits be returned to the Registrar? Dr. Gow, what was the first republic to assert its sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the 1980s, after the death of Tito, there were a series of problems and disputes between the various republics. The first, I think, real assertion of the sovereignty of the republics was by Serbia. This occurred in the mid 1980s where the position of Serbia as a sovereign entity began to be a matter of discussion. This was because of the status of Serbia with the two autonomous provinces. It was said that Serbian's sovereignty was impaired by the imposition, by the creation, of these two autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did it go about doing this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbia, the Serbian authorities began a process of reintegration, of making, of removing the autonomy from the provinces so that Serbia would be, in their terms, a whole sovereign, territorial, integral state form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going back for a moment to the constitutional arrangements that emerged after 1974; was there any distinction between nations and nationalities in the 1974 constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The distinction was made in Articles 3 and 4 of the constitution to which I made reference already in identifying the difference between the republics and the autonomous provinces. The republics endowed with sovereignty were taken to be states which represented the creative power of state forming people. In the Yugoslav terms, these were peoples or nations -- the same word "narod" was used, but clearly can have two different meanings in English and the two meanings are, to some extent, elided in the use in Serbo-Croat. The term "nationality" or, in Serbo-Croat, "narodnost", was used to designate what might more conventionally now be called national minorities, that is, people who were communities with a significant number within the federal boundaries but who were not state forming peoples. This was because they were taken to have a state formed by their people somewhere else. So, for example, the Albanians in Kosovo were not taken to be a state forming people because the Albanian state existed. The state forming peoples of the Yugoslav Federation were peoples who had no state that they could look to in some other place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What powers were left with the Federation in the 1974 constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Federation was, effectively, left with restricted capabilities in the field of some areas of overall economic management, in the area of foreign policy and in the area of overall defence policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did the communist party play in the Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The communist party was central to the running of a state like Yugoslavia. It was central at the federal level but, increasingly, it was the concentration of power in communist hands in the republican structures which consolidated divisions between the various republics within the Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again in the Federation what role did Tito play?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While Tito was alive, again, as I said before, he was always there, both within the party and within the Federal state structures. He was able to resolve difficulties on the basis of his own personal authority derived from the wartime experience derived from the defiance of the Soviet Union in the 1940s. He was the figure who was able to make this system work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these matters that you have just been attesting to again reflected in the 1974 constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tito's importance to the system was reflected in the 1974 constitution and in the party's statutes at the time. In both cases, he was made either President for life or President for an indefinite period which was, effectively, for life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, the power sharing mechanisms between the republics and the Federation, how long did that continue to survive after the 1974 constitution was brought into effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The arrangements of the 1974 constitution could work while Tito was still alive and was there to help make them work. Increasingly, after Tito died in May 1980, the Federation ran into increasing mixture of social, economic, political and eventually constitutional difficulties which could not be resolved, because the basis for any resolution was consensus between the republics; the republics increasingly had polarized views, some of them had polarized views, of what the future should hold. In that situation, the Federation began to break down and to cease to function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, these were some of the factors that led to the ultimate disintegration of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ultimate disintegration of the Federation in the early 1990s was a product of this experience; first of all, of the implementation of the federal system, of the imposition of tight communist control within the federal structures which consolidated power and created state structures, but which eventually gave enough strength to those various republics through the course of the 1980s to begin to be going their own ways in terms of their perspectives on the future, whether the future would be a common future or a future apart from each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to turn to the breakup of the Federation as such. Firstly, I would ask you to look at the document now shown to you. (Handed) Dr. Gow, what is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a version of the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences. This version is published by Nase Teme in Zagreb in, I think, 1988 or it may be 87. The document originally -- the original memorandum of the Serbian Academy circulated in 1985, and the second version was produced in 1986. This is one of the versions which may be available and is in this present form in a translation in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there is an English translation attached to it, is there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And there is an English translation attached behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What purpose was this document prepared for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The status of the document is, I should point out, first of all, may be not authoritative. There were different versions of this document circulating. As I understand it, the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences has never officially published the document. It was a document of an internal discussion group, although it was widely circulated in the mid-1980s, both within the territories of Yugoslavia and outside the territories of the Yugoslav Federation. This, I would take to be, I judge to be, a more authoritative version. The significance of the document is that a group of Serbian intellectuals were clearly beginning to question the nature of the Federation, Serbia's position within it and, as I made reference to the question of Serbian sovereignty earlier, began to address the question of Serbian sovereignty and the need to deal with an unusual position in which Serbia found itself, on the one hand, technically a sovereign state but, on the other, a state with two autonomous provinces which significantly impaired the sovereignty of that republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that document. Document No. 21?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 21 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once the document has been marked, might it be handed back to Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, if it is all material, I wonder if the witness could explain how it is that the existence of the two autonomous states had been effectively impairing the sovereignty of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly, your Honour. I will direct that question now. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, you heard His Honour's question. Perhaps you might address that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed I will. I am grateful that you ask me the question. Under the terms of the 1974 constitution, the two autonomous provinces which in 1946 had been, as all the federal structures had been, nothing more than formal, had also been formal, by 1974 had been given significant de facto powers of self-government. They were different from the republics in that they were not endowed with the quality of sovereignty, but in most other respects they had the capacities, the functions, the structures of a republican state. It was, therefore, regarded within Serbia as a significant factor that Serbia as a whole was supposed to be a state and a sovereign state, but it had two autonomous provinces within it, both of which had such substantial degrees of self-government that the writ of the Serbian government in Belgrade could not run. The two provinces could set their own terms and could veto, in some areas could veto Belgrade's decisions, but Belgrade at that time did not have the capacity to overrule decisions taken by the provinces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now going to Exhibit 21 there, I am looking at pages 321 to 322, if you would not mind, firstly, of the English translation and down towards the bottom of the page, I think, if we can? It may be expanded.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Stephen and I are just talking about those two autonomous provinces; what were the names of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The names were Vojvodina which is in the north and Kosovo which is in the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just to clarify that, they are actually often seen in the boundary of Serbia when one sees the Serbian boundaries drawn

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both provinces are within the Republic of Serbia, and they were indicated on maps that were offered in evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In terms of what is now displayed on the screen, can you tell us the significance of this in terms of the complaint, as it were, that Serbia had in the early stages or the initial complaint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The paragraph at the bottom of the page which I have indicated makes reference to the question I was just dealing with in answer to your Honour's question. The question of the integrity of the Serbian state was identified -- you will see the question of it being virtually divided into three parts -- is raised the way in which the autonomous provinces were de facto given similar powers to republics with the exception that they were not defined as states within that arrangement, and that that position, as you move down the paragraph, means that they, in terms of the way it is expressed here, interfere in the internal affairs of Serbia proper, that Serbia as a whole, they said, could not function because of the existence of these two provinces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that is continued over the page as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you were to move to the very last sentence of the page which continues over, I do not think you need to see it, but it identifies the status of Serbia itself in their eyes is not clearly defined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going on further in that exhibit to page 327, you find that on that page further expression of the Serbian position with respect to the Federation. Perhaps you might like to look at the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You are making it too small.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Read the exhibit first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe you could enlarge the area of this paragraph, the middle paragraph, just make it easier to see. In this paragraph, you can see the way in which among Serbian intellectuals at that time the question was not only of the status and the sovereignty of Serbia, but also of the position of the Serbs living outside of the Republic of Serbia. If you recall, we had some discussion yesterday and on the maps I indicated the spread of Serbian populations across the territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatia. In this paragraph, the question of the way in which the Serbs in other parts of the Federation in Croatia are being assimilated and, therefore, a question of their national identity is being brought into question in the eyes of these intellectuals is identified. If you move to the last sentence of the paragraph, you will see the way in which the Serbian intellectuals at this stage were discussing the integrity of the Serbian people as a whole, the Serbian people throughout the Federation. They were identifying that in the situation in the 1980s with the increasing evolution of the federal system into a set of state structures, the question of Serbs living outside the territory of Serbia itself was to be a significant question. A few lines before that you will see the Serbian people of Croatia are cut off from their parent country, but the parent country has limited possibilities for helping, for finding out what their position really is. So, the significance of this is to identify the interest of the Serbian elite in the position of Serbs outside Serbia itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Dr. Gow, at the very bottom of page 35 over to page 36, looking at page 35 first and highlighting the bottom paragraph, if you could? 35 first and then the final paragraph -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may just go back to the previous pages for one moment, I think it would in the light of things which have happened afterwards and in the light of some of the evidence which I hope to be able to give later, in the final sentence of this paragraph I was dealing with, I would just draw your Honour's attention to the phrase "the integrity of Serbian people", because this was to become a significant feature in events afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, this may not be of tremendous importance, but on the exhibit list, this memorandum is dated 1989. I heard your testimony that you thought it was drafted in 1987 or 1988. Was it then not published or something until 1989? Is that the difference? I am referring to Exhibit 21.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can, yes, if I may clarify? I said that it was drafted originally in 1985, but there was another draft of it in 1986. But, to my knowledge, it was never officially published by the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences itself, but some people from the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences have said that it was never an official document, that it was only a matter of an internal discussion group. One of the versions of that memorandum, that discussion document, was published in a journal in Zagreb in 1988, not 1989 I said, and this is identified -- if I can put this on, I will show you -- that publication date of 1989 is indicated. It is probably too small to read, but it is just there at the top. Sorry, it was published in 1989, but through 1988, so it was 1989. I misread it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In relation to the questions of publication, was there during Tito's Yugoslavia an effort put in by the Federal government to as much as possible maintain any movements for independence of that of the various republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Tito's time there certainly had been moves of that kind. One of the main driving factors which led to the 1974 constitution were moves in Croatia in the late 1960s into the very beginning of the 1970s in a movement which seemed to aspire to independence. One of the reasons for the situation in which the 1974 constitution was adopted was that control was being reinforced in Croatia. This was, of course, also one of the mechanisms which reinforced communist party control in the republics because it was not only in Croatia, it was in all the republics as well, and it was a by-product of that mechanism -- the constitution was one way of addressing that problem, of the Croatian impulse for greater independence at that stage. Control was to be taken by strengthening party structures within the republic, so greater autonomy, greater independence, for the republic was granted, but control was expected to be exercised through the communist party. But in all the republics, increasingly, the communist parties took on their own perspective rather than a Yugoslav Federal communist perspective after Tito's death. If I may continue beyond the Tito period as well, just to indicate that the publication of a document like the memorandum was a cause of great concern in a country such as the federal Yugoslavia was because of the importance of the relations between state communities and between republics. The federal authorities expressed deep concern and tried to prevent the publication of the document and its circulation in the mid 1980s, as did the authorities at that time of the Republic of Serbia who saw it as a potentially dangerous document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, if I can take you to the final paragraph on page 335? Again, do we see in the paragraph a further expression of this feeling of inadequate representation by Serbia as to be singled out from the other republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The final complete sentence on this page indicates -----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the paragraph starting with "However"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The paragraph begins "The fact that", the sentence begins "However, the biggest trouble is that the Serbian people do not have a state while all the other nations or peoples do". The significance of this is again the impaired sovereignty in terms of this document of the Republic of Serbia. Serbia, whilst all the other peoples, the constituent peoples of Yugoslavia, the Slovenes, the Croats, had a titular state, Serbia is said not to have a complete titular state because of the presence of the autonomous provinces; therefore, Serbian statehood is in question, and this is a challenge to the provisions of the 1974 federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might that exhibit be returned to the Registrar? Dr. Gow, as a consequence of the memorandum we have just seen, Exhibit 21, and the nationalist programme itself, was there any reaction to this in Serbia in 1989?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a consequence of this memorandum that had been drawn up, was there a reaction to it in Serbia in 1989?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Increasingly, in the late 1980s in Serbia the question of the position of Serbia itself and of the Serbs within the Yugoslav Federation was being brought into question, and the current President of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, first of all, in the late 1980s became leader of the League of Communists of Serbia, largely on the basis of beginning to address the concerns of intellectuals and of ordinary people about the position of Serbia and the Serbs and, in particular, began to institute a policy of reintegrating the provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just ask you to look at the document which you are now shown. (Handed). What is that document, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a copy of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia from 1974.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where that document is sourced from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the current form, it appears to be derived from, I think it looks from the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia, but it is not indicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will just tender that document, if your Honours please. That is No. 22. Does that have an English translation as well, Dr. Gow, of at least some of the Articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there objection to Exhibit 22?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As far as the English translation is included, no opposition.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have one available?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think the translation of the Articles are at the back, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me. There is not a full translation, but a translation of particular sections is attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, we will not oppose it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 22 then will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, if you could place on the screen, firstly, Article 1, the translated Article 1. By reference to that Article, can you tell us, please, how the autonomous provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina were governed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Article currently displayed indicates that the Socialist Republic of Serbia was identified as a state -- if you move into the second paragraph -- as the state of the Serbian people and the other members of peoples and national minorities in Yugoslavia, and that it was all those people who realised their sovereign rights through the republic as a whole. The final part, if you move down into the next section, it indicates the two autonomous provinces, Vojvodina and Kosovo, were identified as parts of the Socialist Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We learn more about this governing of these provinces out of Articles 291 and 293, if that might be displayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The article currently displayed indicates the self-governing nature of the autonomous provinces, but also identifies that, in theory, they should be acting within the common interest of the people and of the Republic of Serbia as a whole. Should I move on to 293 as well in conjunction? 293 confirms the self-governing status and indicates that it would be a matter for the provincial authorities independently to determine social, legal relations and so forth within that territory, and that those areas would be -- that republican law, although it is applicable throughout the whole of the territory of Serbia, will be to some extent need to be harmonised with the law of the provinces which will independently set legal regulations and political relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might that exhibit be returned? Dr. Gow, did this method of governing the autonomous provinces in Serbia change in 1989?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1989, the central authorities of the Republic of Serbia began a process of removing the autonomy of the two provinces which was to lead eventually to the full removal of authority on 28th September 1990, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the changes in the method of government of the autonomous provinces affected? How was it achieved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was achieved on one level through legal means because the provincial parliamentary bodies themselves were used to vote to remove the authority of the provinces, but prior to that the Serbian President had also installed within the communist party structures people who were prepared to guide the policy in that direction and to help in the process of removing it. When the eventual vote on the removal of the autonomy, or elements of the autonomy, of Kosovo was taken, it was under a considerable degree of threat, and elements of Serbian and Federal Interior Ministry and I believe also Yugoslav People's Army, armed forces, were deployed in the area and around the parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing with the legal means, would you look at this document that you are now shown? (Handed) I think there is attached to it a translation of part of the document, an English translation of part of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is decisions on proclamation of amendments to the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, and it is taken from the Sluzbeni Glasnik, official gazette of the Republic of Serbia, and there is, indeed, an English translation attached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just while you have the document there, were these legal changes to the methods of governing the provinces reflected particularly in amendments 31 and 33 as is attained in the English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I tender that, your Honour. That is No. 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 23 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Also dealing with a similar topic, would you look, please, at the document you are now shown? (Handed) What is this document, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a copy of an English version of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia from 1990 published in the same series, Oceana Publications, Constitutions of Dependancies and Special Sovereignties, to which reference was made earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that on page 11 -- just to take, if I may, page 11 for the moment -- do you see that the introduction part of this document has been signed by a Professor Markovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, if any, what role Professor Markovic had? Firstly, where does Professor Markovic come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Professor Markovic works in the University of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, if any, what role he had in relation to this constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had some role there drafting the constitution, I believe, and was responsible for writing the commentary which is attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that exhibit, your Honour. It is No. 24.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Exhibit 24 by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 24 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once that document is marked, might the exhibit be handed back to Dr. Gow? (To the witness): Dr. Gow, just looking at page 5 for me, if you would -- I want to show you a couple of pages in this memorandum, in this exhibit, but starting firstly with page 5 -- in your opinion, does this extract demonstrate with respect to some of the issues raised in the SANU memorandum and, if so, by the reference to the extracts, can you demonstrate how this was sought to be achieved to overcome some of those problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The most significant part of this is the first sentence which indicates that, in the view of Professor Markovic as a drafter of the constitution, the constitution which reflects the complete integration of the two provinces within republican structures is also a way after many years of restoring dignity within the whole Yugoslav framework to constitutions as legal mechanisms. I think, although Professor Markovic goes on to talk about a number of other factors, I think the important thing to understand the question of dignity, I would regard, as being central to the understanding of the changes in the constitution were, in Serbian eyes, to be seen as restoring dignity to Serbia and, therefore, to the functioning of a constitutional system as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, Dr. Gow, it is not necessary for these to be displayed necessarily, unless you think it would assist, but I think there are further references to this on pages 9, 10 and 11; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On page 9, Professor Markovic goes on to point out that, according to the new constitution of Serbia, only one state exists, as everywhere else in the world, as the territory of the single state of Serbia, and this is something which is natural and as it should be; again re-emphasising the question of the previous questions about the sovereignty and territorial integrity and so forth of Serbia, and now judged to have been addressed by the new constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Can you please point to the relevant parts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can indeed, yes, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The paragraph that I am just indicating, it reads, "According to the new constitution of Serbia, only one state does exist, as everywhere else in the world", and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might show us page 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The final paragraph raises the question of the constitutional status of Serbia within the Federation. It addresses the question that by creating a strong Serbian constitution, it may have turned its back on the forms of the Federal Yugoslavia established under the 1974 constitution. It indicates that in the eyes of Professor Markovic he would want to say that it has only made the relations between Serbia and the Federation more precise, that they continue for the time being to recognise the primacy of the federal constitution, but do begin, as you move on to page 11, to indicate the possibility of some other non-federal Yugoslavia, although he also goes on to say that it is beyond the interest of Serbia at this stage. If you move further into this paragraph, I think you will see that Serbia is beginning to prepare for the dissolution of Yugoslavia, and it is preparing in what it would regard as self-defence to take actions which might include what it would regard as defence, what it would formally at least regard as defence, move away from the Federal constitution; if it sees any violations of the Federal constitution which it would regard as being detrimental to Serbia, it would take action in self-defence, namely, "republic authorities shall issue acts in order to protect the interest of the Republic of Serbia".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might the exhibit be returned? Dr. Gow, did the events in Kosovo have any influence over what happened in other parts of the Federation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did. In the process of overall disintegration in relations between the republics of the Federation, the events in Kosovo in the way autonomy was removed from Kosovo, in particular, encouraged those in other parts of the Federation to begin to think in terms of mechanisms of self-protection. There was an increasing fear that what had happened in Kosovo and in Vojvodina might be part of a programme from the Serbian leadership in Belgrade to expand its control throughout the Federation. Therefore, increasingly the question of measures, including the possibility of independence, was being discussed in other republics, in contrast to the developments in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just remind us again, what time frame are we talking about, what particular time frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are talking about the period in the second half of the 1980s, particularly 1988 and afterwards and increasingly through 1989 and into the beginning of the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know you have touched on it briefly, but remind us again. Apart from the legal moves that we have just examined through the documents, what other events happened in terms of Kosovo and Vojvodina to influence the other republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The changes in the constitutional arrangements were enacted in part because the republic of -- the League of Communists of Serbia had also taken control, effective control, of the communist parties in the areas, or was taking control of during this period, and also because in the case of Kosovo there was a presence of various types of armed force. There were a series of protests from the predominantly Albanian population, and significant numbers of Albanians were killed in clashes with police and with Federal security forces. It was a very tense situation, and when the autonomy of Kosovo was finally removed, it was in a situation where armoured vehicles were deployed in the area around the Kosovo Parliament in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the principal architect for removing this autonomy of Kosovo? Who was primarily behind this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The then leader of League of Communists of Serbia, the current President of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, was regarded as being the main instigator of these changes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving now to Bosnia, upon what lines were the political parties at this particular time constituted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a difficult situation, as the process of disintegration, I think, was beginning to be well underway throughout the territories of the SFRY, increasingly there was a tendency for parties to take a nationalist character. So there were a series of elections held in 1990, first of all, in Slovenia and then through other republics in the course of the year, all of which tended to lead in politics of a nationalist character within Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, broadly, a mixture of national communist and nationalist parties were elected in a coalition in Slovenia; a nationalist party was elected with a very strong vote in Croatia; a similar pattern throughout the whole of the territories of the Federation; in Serbia and Montenegro, the two communist parties were re-elected, in the case of Serbia, under a new name, the Socialist Party of Serbia, but with a very strong again nationalist content to its policy. Within Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was the most mixed of all the states which made up the Yugoslav Federation, politics began to divide along the lines of ethno-national communities. So when elections were held, the votes went broadly to three ethno-nationally conceived parties, to the Muslim Party of Democratic Action, to the Serbian Democratic Party and to the Croatian branch of the Croatian Democratic Community; each of these parties at that stage adopting some kind of line, some kind of policy, which reflected, ostensibly at least, the interests of a particular ethno-national community within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For our assistance, can you tell us the initials that are often attached to these various political parties in Bosnia, starting perhaps with the Muslim Party of Democratic Action, what is the traditional initials one sees for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim Party of Democratic Action is usually referred to or is often referred to as the "SDA", Stranka Demokratske Akcije, and is led by the current President of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Itzebegovic. The Serbian democratic party is usually referred to as the "SDS", Srpska Demokratska Stranka, and is led by Mr. Radovan Karadzic. The Croatian Democratic Community, which is also the name of the party led by President Franjo Tudjman of Croatia, has a branch in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The initials for that are usually "HDZ", Hrvatska Demokratska Zajednica, and the leader at this time was a man called Stjepan Kljuic. Since then the leadership has changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these parties then elect a President of the presidency? Perhaps you might explain what that means in terms of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was a collective body. It was the ruling body. It had no single President. It had a rotating leadership, as was also the case, I indicated earlier, with the Federation itself. That body elected from its number (which I think was seven but I am not certain about that) as President of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the first period before rotation Alija Itzebegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in Serbia while this was happening in Bosnia, were there elections then held in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the elections held in Serbia at the end of 1990 resulted in substantial victory for the renamed communist party, the Socialist Party of Serbia under the leadership of Slobodan Milosovic. Similarly, the League of Communists of Montenegro which had not changed its name also won a substantial victory under the leadership of Momir Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, what did the results of these elections mean for Yugoslavia in terms of the Federation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The outcome of the elections in various republics confirmed the degree to which each of the republics had a separate character, the degree to which they were moving in different directions and the degree to which that direction was characterised by a perception of the republic's national interests or, in some cases, perhaps, the interests of the predominant titular group within the republic. It was certainly paving the way for the dissolution which was to come within a couple of years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other signs of this dissolution of the Yugoslavia emerging at around about this time? I am talking in terms of the early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the breakdown in the relations between the republics as the federating states was taking place, and the consequence of the nationalist parties coming to power more or less in all the republics, there also began to be a breakdown in social relations, in relations at an intercommunal level in certain parts of the territories of the SFRY, in particular, in areas of Croatia in 1990, following the election of the HDZ government of President Franjo Tudjman who took certain measures, particularly with regard to adopting a new constitution and restructuring the Interior Ministry, which began to cause concern against the background of the arguments between the different republican leaderships. This gave rise to growing intercommunal tension, to the sense that the Serbs living -- who in some areas of Croatia with a majority population were beginning to be alienated -- this is Serbs living in those areas as opposed to Serbs who might still be living in urban areas, such as the capital in Zagreb -- began to become alienated, there certainly began to be problems within those communities in relations between Serbs and Croats. In 1990 there were a series of incidents, some involving violence, which began to lead to the deployment of Federal army troops in the area to take control. At the same time there were fewer but growing incidents of a similar nature in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So at the same time as there was this breakdown in state relations, there was also beginning to be a breakdown in communal relations within some of the states of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Krajina Serbs react in any way to the moves taken by President Tudjman regarding the restructuring of the Croatian Interior Ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In response to the Croatian government's adoption of a new constitution in which the status of the Serbian people was apparently changed, and in response to the attempts to reorganise the Interior Ministry, attempts which were on the one hand aimed at getting rid of communists who were in those state structures, but also was a mechanism of getting rid of Serbs. It is very difficult for anybody to say whether they were getting rid of communists or Serbs because the two happened to be the same in that context. It was certainly a move which made some of the Serbs in the Krajina area begin to feel a sense of threat, and it was a situation in which, with backing from Belgrade and in some cases with the assistance from the Yugoslav People's Army, that local Serbs began to declare autonomous regions. In the course of 1990, they declared two autonomous regions, one of Krajina, and the other of Eastern Slovenia, Western Srem and Baranja. In these two areas they began to create, certainly in the area of the Krajina, what was a de facto no-go area for any Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask for clarification of this. I gather "Krajina" means "border" and there is an old tradition of Serbs guarding the border in Krajina against the Turks, is that the origin?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps, Dr. Gow, you might assist His Honour with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be glad to; if I may, I would prefer to do it also with the assistance of a map, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Do it at an appropriate time -- not necessarily now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think now would be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps this map, which is Exhibit 2, could be displayed on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The word "Krajina" means "frontier". The areas on the borders here indicated of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, as I indicated yesterday, for most of the period of a few hundred years formed the frontier area between the two Empires, the Austro-Hungarian Hapsburg Empire and the Turkish Ottoman Empire. The term "Krajina", or the term "Vojna Krajina" means "military frontier", and it was an area which extended from the Dalmatian hinterland around here, all the way along the borders of Croatia and Bosnia, through Vojvodina (as was then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire) and up into parts of Timasoara and what is today Rumania. The area as a whole was a military frontier area. It had a mixed population. In areas Serbs were the predominant population. The arrangements for the people living in those areas were that they would have special tax privileges, they would have certain concessions. They would live there, they would use the land there on condition that in time of need they would be the frontiersmen who would guard the frontier. In the particular case of relationship between predominantly Serbian populations and the Croatian Sabor -- that is the kind of parliament that was there within Croatia within the Austro-Hungarian Empire -- there were often difficulties because the Sabor in Zagreb wanted to have taxation control and so forth of the people in those areas, but in fact those people had special status given to them by Vienna, vis-a-vis things like the conditions in which they lived there. They did not have a special status beyond that, and they were not exclusively Serb, but it was mixed areas which included Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, Rumanians, Hungarians which stretched all the way along that border up into what is presently Rumania. But the word "krajina" means "frontier" and the Vojna Krajina was the military frontier area which ran along there, and the term "krajina" is used to refer to a part of that territory now, the part in the Dalmation hinterland around there, which in 1990/91 had majority Serbian populations in something like six of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps just to finish that off, is a frontier from whom against what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the frontier, as I said, between the Austro-Hungarian Hapsburg Empire and Turkish Ottoman Empire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, a moment ago we were talking about the various moves, both political and otherwise, in relation to the beginning of the breakup of Yugoslavia and, in particular, the reference to the elections and so forth that were being held. Were there at this particular time any proposals advanced in order to try to deal with the developing political crisis in the 1990s, early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of the first part of the 1990s, different ideas were being proposed about the future of relations within the Federation between the republics. The main ideas were that of a modernised Federation which was proposed by Borisav Jovic who was the Serbian representative to the Federal collective presidency. This was, essentially, for a strengthened, more centralised version of the existing Federation. An alternative idea put forward by Slovenia and by Croatia was that of a formalised confederation. Some people regarded this only as a vehicle for engineering the break up of the Federation. The final -- an alternative in 1991 which was proposed at a late stage was an asymmetric Federation proposed by the leaders of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of Macedonia, which was to see a la carte federation or confederation; everybody would stay part of a Yugoslav framework, but take as much of it as they wanted. Against this background also, you had the then federal prime minister, Ante Markovic, who was the last federal prime minister, who was trying to ignore the growing problems in each of the republics and trying to engineer an economic reform programme which in the first part 1990 was appearing to be very successful, but in the second part of 1990 became less successful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Serbia's position in all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbia, reflecting the fact that Borisav Jovic proposed the modernised federation favoured stronger centralisation of the federation, removing significant degrees of independence from the republics, concentrating power again in Belgrade, and it, therefore, opposed the proposals of the Slovenian and Croatian confederalists to consolidate power within the republics and to confirm the de facto arrangements which had emerged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, yes. We will stand in recess for 15 minutes. (11.30 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Dr. Gow, before the adjournment you were discussing the attempts made, the various proposals put forward in order to, in an effort to try to save the fragmenting federation. I think that you touched on the fact that the Prime Minister at the time of the Federation of Yugoslavia, Prime Minister Markovic, had also put forward a proposal himself. Perhaps you could just touch back on that again and tell us what the fate of his proposals were that he had advanced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure it would be accurate to say that he put forward a proposal as such. He favoured the continuation of some kind of community for, Yugoslavia whether it be federation or confederation, it did not matter what, so long as they returned a single economic space. He attempted to make that possible through the economic reform programme he initiated in the first part of 1990. In the second part of 1990 the successors which were apparent in the first part of the year, reducing inflation from somewhere over 2,600 per cent, even down to zero, on a monthly basis, still did not provide the basis upon which to build any kind of renewed arrangement between the Yugoslav republics. I think the reason for that is essentially that none of the republics were willing from their own different perspectives to support that kind of a programme, whether it was from Belgrade or from Ljubija, the Slovenian capital, each had its own perspective and had no interest in supporting Markovic in the efforts to create an economic policy by which a community of Yugoslavs could be sustained in that way. Each had other interests and, therefore, was not giving its support to the federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what happened to Slovenia or what happened in Slovenia in December 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In December 1990 the Slovenian authorities authorised a referendum on the question of Slovenia's possible independence. That referendum was overwhelmingly supported, supported the proposition that Slovenia should become independent if there were not to be a suitable accommodation between the Yugoslav republics within six months, and the Slovenia authorities proceeded to act in making preparations from that point onwards for independence, whilst continuing with some discussions about the possibility of a continuing Yugoslav community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the document that I am now showing. What is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It as an extract from the Uradni list, the official gazette of the Republic of Slovenia, and it is a record of the outcome of the referendum and there is an English translation attached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this translation one can see the overwhelming vote in favour of the question for separation, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can indeed, yes. You see that an overwhelming majority of those voting voted for the independence of the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that document, if your Honours please. It is document No. 25.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you show it on the screen, Dr. Gow? Is there any objection to Exhibit 25?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 25 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information is all contained on one page in the original extract. In the translation it goes over two pages. The first page indicates those who were eligible to vote and those who did take part in the plebescite. The second page here indicates the total number of voting papers handed in, and here indicates the total number of those who voted "yes" to the question whether the Republic of Slovenia should become an independent and sovereign state. Immediately below that is given the figures for those who voted "no", and finally voting papers which were spoiled in some way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, in your opinion, when did the Federation of Yugoslavia cease to function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although it is an extremely difficult question for anybody to be precise about, I would say that probably the federation ceased to function on 15th May 1991, at which point the procedure for the appointment of the President of the collective presidency of the federation broke down. That procedure was an automatic annual rotation in a set order as laid out in laws passed pursuant to the 1974 constitution, and at that stage it should have passed from the Serbian representative Borisav Jovic to the Croatian representative who at that time was Stjepan Mesic, but for the first time a formal vote was actually called on the question of the rotation and the four representatives controlled by the Republic of Serbia following the changes to the internal structure of Serbia, so they were able to call on the votes of Montenegro as well as the two autonomous provinces, blocked the rotation and I think it is from at that point onwards you can say that the federation had clearly ceased to function as a federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true to say that from at that time onwards the federation lacked a head of state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be true to say that the formal head of state of the SFRY following the death of Tito was the President of the presidency, and that in the situation where there was no President of the presidency then, technically, Yugoslavia would be without a formal head of state, although it would have, it would continue notionally to have the collective head of state which was the presidency itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might -- can you just elaborate a little bit for us on how Serbia was able to achieve this in terms of voting numbers and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will recapitulate. Because of the changes which had taken place both within party structures but, more importantly, by this stage within state structures and administrative structures, the Republic of Serbia was able to call on not only its own vote but the vote of Montenegro where Serbia was judged to have responsible in changing the leadership in course of 1989 and bringing Bulatovic into power as an eye of President Milosevic and also on the votes of Kosovo and Vojvodina because as a result of the changes those representatives were now de facto taken to be representatives not so much of the provinces themselves but of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact Serbia had four votes whereas the other republics had one that it could marshal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it could be said -- what you could say is that Serbia had more or less complete control with three votes in that situation and could count on the fourth vote of Montenegro. It is a significant that, although the effective autonomy of the two provinces was removed, the representation of the two provinces in the collective federal presidency was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the President of the presidency that should have taken over was a Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. That was Stipe Mesic who was the Croatian representative to the federation at that time, to the collective federal presidency at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Croatia do when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatia obviously was thrown into a degree of consternation and within four days went ahead with a referendum which it had called on the question of Croatia's prospective independence. Although the decision to hold the referendum had been taken perhaps a week or two, I forget the exact date but shortly before that, the effective, the effect of the events of 15th May were to catalyze the referendum question immediately prior to its being held, and to make it clear, if it were not clear before that, to the Croats that they would support the question of Croatian independence. I suspect they would have done so overwhelmingly anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at the document I am now showing you. (Handed). What is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
