utterances.text: This is the Narodne novine which is again the official gazette of the Republic of Croatia, and it is an extract from that document which indicates the decision to call a referendum on the question of Croatian independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That extract, is there an English translation of the extract that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might display that on the screen for us, please? I think that is item No. 646, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision on calling a referendum. You see that two questions were posed on the future of Croatia's relations: whether or not that it should be an independent and sovereign state but holding out the possibility that it could join a federation with other republics within the context of the confederal proposals made by Slovenia and Croatia, and a second question which asks whether or not the Republic of Croatia should stay within Yugoslavia as constituted with the SFRY on the terms proposed by the proposal I indicated by Borisav Jovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before we get too deep into that exhibit, is there any objection? I guess not. Exhibit 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 26 then will be admitted. I did not mean to stop you testifying regarding the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Following these referendums, Dr. Gow, did Slovenia and Croatia issue declarations of independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may first just add that there was an overwhelming vote in Croatia as well for the independence of Croatia as expressed in the terms of the questions put, and on 25th June 1991 both Slovenia and Croatia declared their independence from the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that reflected in the document now shown to you? What is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is reflected in the document which is from the Uradni list from the Republic of Slovenia and is the text of the declaration of independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the source of this document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the source of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I indicated it came from Uradni list, the official gazette of the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I tender that exhibit, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Exhibit 27?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 27 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said there was also a similar declaration in relation to Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps looking at the exhibit, at the next document which you are shown, (Handed), is this also -- well, tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is again an extract from the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia, and it contains the constitutional decision on the sovereignty and independence of the Republic of Croatia on 20th June 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a reference in that document to -- sorry, is there an English translation accompanying that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is an English translation accompanying the document, and that English translation is taken from Yugoslav Survey No. 3 1991 published by the federal authorities of the SFRY in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Exhibit 28?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 28 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what was the effect of these declarations of independence that you have just been referring to in Exhibits 27 and 28 which have been tendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The declarations of independence raised in a definite and possibly final way the future, any possible future for a Yugoslav community. It indicated clearly the intention of the republics of Slovenia and Croatia to become independent. It raised the question of the status of the other Yugoslav republics, and it gave rise to the process, the final process of disintegration including armed conflict of which we are all only too well aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Republic of Serbia, what was its position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia formally continued to support the existence of the SFRY, although de facto appeared, the Serbian President appears to have come to a limited understanding, if not a formal agreement, with the leader of the Republic of Slovenia, Milan Kucan, on Slovenia's possible future. But, essentially, the Republic of Serbia opposed, formally opposed the breakup.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps looking, if you would for me, at document 29, can you tell me what that document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is an extract from the constitutions of the countries of the world, Oceania Publications series referred to earlier, and concerns the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is the label adopted by Serbia and Montenegro following the collapse of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the effect of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The effect of the document given here, which is the calculation of that Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by the leaderships, the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro, was to confirm the end of the SFRY as was, if there was any remaining question as to the existence of the SFRY, and therefore absolutely to complete a process of disintegration of the SFRY. So between the end, between the point at which I would say the federation finally ceased to function on 15th May 1991, the point at which Slovenia and Croatia indicated that they regarded it as no longer functioning and declared their independence on 25th June 1991, and this declaration which was issued on 27th April 1992 the SFRY went through a process of dissolution, which process, if not before, was finally complete on 27th April 1992 when this declaration was issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 29 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps after it is marked it can be given to the witness. I will just get you to point to the actual declaration itself and the date of the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would first indicate the title of the document as a whole is "Declaration", and that if you move to paragraph 1 and the sentence before it, "The representatives of the people of the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro declare the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and they claimed the continued state, international, legal, political personality of the former SFRY".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask a question? Does that mean that the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by its creation acknowledged the fact that neither Croatia nor Slovenia were a part of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that would be an accurate reading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Acknowledged also that they were independent states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that that is the case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You perhaps might just show us the date that appears on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date, as you see, is Belgrade on April 27th 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, after this declaration, the last one that we have just seen, what then followed in what was former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the declaration of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I would say that there then followed -- there had already been a period of armed conflict, but through the sum of all the declarations to which we have made reference, including the final declaration of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was the formal disappearance of the SFRY and the onset and continuation of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, if I can pursue that last question? Where did that leave Bosnia-Herzegovina, if it was excluded specifically from the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, yet had not declared independence from the old Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina had declared independence from the old SFRY, and I believe that in the course of the evidence to come we will be indicating that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It had occurred by this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it had occurred by this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would like now to move over to a consideration of what was the military position in Yugoslavia, in particular, the Yugoslav People's Army in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I would ask you to start with an examination of this Army leading up to the time of the breakup and thereafter. Firstly, under the constitution what was the position of the armed forces of Yugoslavia at the commencement of the armed conflict in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The armed forces of Yugoslavia comprised two elements. The first element was a regular armed force, the Yugoslav People's Army and the designation "people's" should be noted; this reflects the communist orientation of the SFRY. Sometimes these days, because the term "narod" also means "people" and "nation", you will see it translated as "national". It had a very specific connotation of "narod" meaning people for the people's republics, in the same way that there were people's republics in the other communist countries of Central and Eastern Europe in the postwar period. The other element was a territorial element which was organised to be an adjunct to the defence of the country in times of war and which was organised at a republican level. The Federal Army was organised by a Federal Secretariat for People's Defence and the Territorial Defence was organised by republican secretariats, although both were intended to act for the same purpose in defence of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with this, might the witness be shown Exhibit 19? Dr. Gow, I would ask you to go particularly to Article 240? (Handed) Just looking at Article 240, by reference to that particular Article, what is its significance in terms of the position of the armed forces in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second paragraph, as I will indicate now, confirms the two-tier structure I was just indicating. The first paragraph also indicates that the armed forces were given a particular constitutional -- a particular and explicit constitutional role, not only to protect the country from external threat, but also to protect the sovereignty, territorial integrity and social system established by the present constitution, that is, the 1974 constitution of the SFRY. So, the Yugoslav People's Army was given a particular role, a constitutional role, at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The exhibit, if it may stay with -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If I may understand this? In Article 240, the first paragraph, when it says, "... shall protect the independent sovereignty, territorial integrity and the social system of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia established by the present constitution", the constitution provided what now, that the nation would consist not only of Serbia within its territorial boundaries, but also all peoples located within the former Yugoslavia? Is that the meaning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This refers not to the Republic of Serbia, Serbia specifically, but to the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the federation of the six states. The constitutional prerogative of the Yugoslav People's Army (as I read it from this Article) was to be given a role in preserving that federal structure and the socialist self-managing system, if you like, the communist party system, that was instituted throughout the Federation. So it was given a task not only of preserving the independence of the country from external threat, but also of preserving the internal relationships established by this 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me again what were the internal relationships established by the constitution, at least in terms of the relationship between Serbian peoples located outside of the territorial boundaries of Serbia, if anything -- maybe I am confused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not clear that it was given any particular role in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. That is the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not see that that was a part of the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps the exhibit might stay with the witness as I wish to refer to it a little later on? (To the witness): Dr. Gow, what was the intended purpose of the two-tiered system of armed forces in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The intention of the first tier of the Yugoslav People's Army was to be the first echelon of defence in the event of an attack on the SFRY. Its purpose was simply to try to perform a holding action, maybe for 48 hours or more, to give time for the second element, the Territorial Defence forces to be mobilized. The purpose of that Territorial Defence force was to fulfil the remit of the doctrine of General People's Defence. This was, essentially, a doctrine of defence which would rely on mass armed resistance, normally in guerrilla movements, a movement which was aimed to deter any attack because it would hold out the promise that any attack on the SFRY would be met with a long, difficult campaign which might be initially successful in removing the first echelon of defence, but would be fighting a guerrilla force for a long period afterwards. So it was aimed in the first instance to try to deter attack by persuading anybody that an attack would be too difficult to accomplish and, in the second instance, by making provision to provide the kind of defence if somebody went ahead with an attack -- to provide the kind of defence I have described if somebody went ahead with an attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the historical explanation of having this two-tiered system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One element of the explanation for it goes back to the Second World War, to the tradition of partisan warfare which gave rise to the creation of the Yugoslav People's Army and of communist rule in Federal Yugoslavia. The partisans had been successful in the early parts of the war using these kinds of guerrilla tactic as part of their overall strategy. Of course, while the war was continuing, as they became more successful, that largely guerrilla force was transformed into a more regular force. But the idea that external opponents could be combated through this guerilla type warfare was an important factor in this being an element in post 1945 Yugoslavia's defence system. The particular type of Territorial Defence as defined under the doctrine of General People's Defence came in after 1968. While there had been a particular kind of Territorial Defence force as a reserve element for the regular army until that stage, the nature changed in 1968 when a more real sense that there could be an invasion, I think, was present following the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, real measures were taken, and these included the authority being established within the republics to organise Territorial Defence on the territory of the republics. This is because if there were to be a real attack, there would be a need to fall back and to have local political control. Overall political control would not be able to be guaranteed in the event of an attack, and it was thought that an attack might be a real prospect, so real measures were taken to respond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, was there an ethnic balance in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an ethnic -- within the JNA, as the Yugoslav People's Army, Jugoslavenska Narodna Armija, and within the JNA there was a balance on one level in the conscript kada, and the conscript kada reflected the distribution of ethnic communities throughout the territories of the SFRY. So, the conscript kada would reflect the proportion of, for example, Serbs or, for example, Croats in the population as a whole between 18 and 24. That would be the proportion of each community within the conscript kada. Within the officer corps, the regular elements, there was not such a reflection of the population as a whole, but there was an attempt through a system known as the "key system", "ethnic key system", to try to maintain a balance between representatives of the different ethno-national communities at least in the higher echelons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this ethnic question also reflected in the constitution itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might display Article 242 of Exhibit 19 which you have there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can indicate Article 242 of the constitution, you will see there was the intention with regard to the composition of the officer corps and the question of promotion to try to maintain the principle of the most proportional representation of the republics and autonomous provinces. So there was an intention to try to maintain a proportional balance within the officer corps between individuals from each of the parts of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the position with respect to the Territorial Defence Force itself in terms of its command vis-a-vis the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence Forces were organised by republican secretariats for defence. That organisation took place, at least to some extent, in conjunction with representatives of the JNA, took place in conjunction with representatives of the JNA, and in time of war it was envisaged that, as far as possible, the Territorial Defence Forces would be integrated with units of the JNA, but recognised also that in the situation of isolated groups fighting a guerilla campaign, command would be with local, political military leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What status did the JNA have in the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, the JNA -- I believe I may have indicated this already this morning -- had a position of having the representation equal to that of an autonomous province within the central committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. The central committee of the League of Communists was, effectively, the key body in which the elements of the Federation were -- within the party structures the elements of the Federation were represented. Within a communist party system it could almost be said to be more equivalent to a sovereign parliament than the parliament itself in de facto terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, following on from that, was the JNA given a political role in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was given a political role in the sense of being given this formal membership of the key, central body of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. I believe its political role was wider than that. The Federal Secretary for Defence, who was always the top General in the army, also became a de facto ex-officio member of the collective Federal presidency, was always present or nearly always present at meetings -- I cannot say for sure absolutely always -- and also the JNA was charged, going back to its constitutional role and maybe giving a little bit of expansion and interpretation to that role, was also in some sense charged with being Tito's successor. The idea was that being a body with an interest in the Federation as a whole, rather than an exclusive interest in any one of the republics, it would be able to continue the role which Tito had played as representing the interest of a Federation as a whole. Tito and the Army worked together in 1971 in dealing with the problems in Croatia, to which I made reference earlier, when there were some signs of Croatian movements towards greater independence. From that point onwards, I believe Tito saw the Army as being a possible way of preparing for a Yugoslav presence after his death -- I should also say Yugoslav and communist presence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He saw the JNA playing a role in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would think that Tito clearly saw that the JNA would play a role within the Federation, being a voice within those parties and other bodies which would represent Federal Yugoslav interests rather than those of individual republics or provinces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the forces of disintegration of the Federation that you have attested to earlier in the Federation of Yugoslavia have any impact upon the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the events of the late 1980s and 1990s were underway, the JNA was obviously coming under certain pressures and strains. It was a multi-ethnic army comprised of all the different communities on the territories of the SFRY. Whilst its orientation was towards the Federation, it could not avoid being subject to the pressures both in relationships between the republics and in relationships between the different communities. So, therefore, there were tensions which were leading to a change in the character of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there changes in the organisation of the military forces as a consequence of these forces of disintegration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some changes which came as a consequence of those pressures. There were some changes, perhaps, which may or may not have done. From the end of 1988, the JNA was reorganised. This reorganisation created five military districts. That reorganisation (as we may make reference to later) was significant when it came to the dissolution of the SFRY and the use of armed forces. Beyond that, clearly, the pressures that were working upon the JNA led to a change in its character. It led to rely increasingly on Serbian elements within the JNA as increasingly non-Serbian individuals, groups, began either not to go to do their military service or began to be regarded as being unreliable, slightly difficult elements, within the structures of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned military districts; what relevance, if any, did these changes have to the events of 1990 and beyond?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The particular relevance was that within those changes in the military structures, first, there was a degree of devolution of authority. As a part of the changes, it was envisaged that there would be greater local command in particular situations, so greater authority was transferred to lower levels, more initiative was left there. This was perhaps -- I stress "perhaps" -- to be significant. For example, in the Republic of Croatia during 1990 and 1991, where elements of the local Knin corps, quite clearly, were co-operating with local Serbs in allowing them to obtain weaponry from JNA stores, which is a measure which I say perhaps may only be a matter of the local commanders as part of the locally devolved authority. It was also significant in that the changes in boundaries of the military districts extended, for example, the boundary of the 1st military district from being previously the boundary -- extended the boundary of the first military district. Previously, the boundary was that between the province of Vojvodina and the Republic of Croatia, the province of Vojvodina in northern Serbia, and the Republic of Croatia. That boundary was extended to cover territory on the western side of that border within the Republic of Croatia. It was in the boundaries of that military district, for example, there was a lot of armed activity in 1991, particularly focusing around the town of Vukovar. That activity was being conducted under the auspices of the 1st military district of the then JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, if you would, please, look at the document that you are now shown? Perhaps that exhibit, Exhibit 19, might be returned? Dr. Gow, what I have now handed to you, what is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is a book entitled "Moje Vidjenje Raspada", which is "My view of the collapse" or "disintegration". The author is General Veljko Kadijevic who was Federal Secretary for Defence at the period in which we are talking, through the early 1990s through to the beginning of 1992, and therefore the top general in the army in 1991 when the armed conflict began on the territories of the former Yugoslavia. This book is his view of the collapse, if you like, his account, memoirs, of what took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is the gentleman that you were referring to that would participate in decisions of the Federation almost in a coequal state to the republics? I may have expressed that badly, but if you follow what I mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He, as Federal Secretary for Defence, was part of the Federal government and would be party to decisions of the Federal government and would also be the ex-officio representative to meetings of the Collective Federal Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there an English translation that accompanies that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I tender that exhibit, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Exhibit 30?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objections, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 30 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After that exhibit is marked, could it please be handed back to the witness? Firstly, if you would just put the first page on the screen of the Croatian version -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is probably somewhere -- it is more a Serbo-Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the photograph of the person there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the cover page of the book and this is General Kadijevic photographed for the cover of the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask you to go, if you would, please, to page 61 of the English translation of the book. Perhaps you might just look at it first before it goes on the screen? Perhaps you might tell us the significance there of what appears on that page in terms of the evidence you have just given concerning the break up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, I will try to indicate?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be highlighted, that section there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, General Kadijevic indicates that by the time of his writing in 1991, we no longer had a real common Yugoslav state. Further down, he indicates that for the JNA the position was in practical terms, what this meant in practical terms, and that would be protecting and defending the Serb people outside Serbia and assembling the JNA within the borders of the future Yugoslavia. The future Yugoslavia would be a set of territories which would comprise parts of not only Serbia and Montenegro as understood in these terms, but also parts of the republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I take you to another page, page 72?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What was that page again now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was page 61, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: English translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That appears from this portion that we have in front of us, the parts of Bosnia and Croatia would be included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am adding the interpretation for the purposes -- when the General writes "the border" here, he writes "within the borders of the future Yugoslavia". The borders of the future Yugoslavia are not designated in this portion of the text. They can be derived from understanding of other parts of the text.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That really was the question I was trying to articulate earlier. When you spoke about the two different elements within the Yugoslav Army, the JNA, and you said that one was the regular Army and the other was the Territorial Defence, what I was trying to do was to link the responsibility of the Territorial Defence element of the JNA with the vision of Serbia as reflected in the constitution of Serbia. Perhaps that is not possible, but if you look at exhibit, I think, is it 24, when I thought there was reference to Serbia not just constituting -- I can give you any of the exhibits that you talked about yesterday, the Exhibit 2, I guess it is -- not just that particular geographical western border, but also within the meaning of the constitution, peoples located in other areas of former Yugoslavia. If that is what the constitution, at least -- maybe I am misunderstanding -- was focusing on as constituting Serbia, then when you put on top of that the responsibility of that portion of the JNA, that is, the Territorial Defence element -- you are frowning because you do not understand at all what I am saying -- then would that envision then a portion of the JNA engaging in military activity outside of the defined territorial boundary of Serbia on behalf of peoples who constitute Serbian descent located outside of that border? Do you understand that convoluted question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not absolutely certain, but maybe if I attempt to address it we can establish if I have.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what you have said, really, that this document is talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I need to make clear that the JNA was not the army of the Republic of Serbia; it was the army of the SFRY ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- of which the Republic of Serbia was one element. The Republic of Serbia did not constitutionally or, I think, in any other sense include the Serbs outside the Republic of Serbia, those Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatia. The responsibility, the constitutional responsibility, of the JNA and the political role it was given was with regard to the SFRY as a whole. Its role, that is, the community of states of the six states and of the various peoples. The term "people" is used, as I think I have said already, somewhat ambiguously sometimes because the same word in Serbo-Croat "narod" can be used for an ethno-national nation, ethno-national group people and for a people as in the ordinary people or the people inhabiting the borders of a state. When we looked at the 1974 constitution of the Republic of Serbia, I indicated clearly that it said that the Republic of Serbia was the state of the Serbian people and of the other groups all exercising their sovereignty, saying that it was the people of the territory of the republic. But, quite clearly, the ambiguity has led to questions arising, particularly with people who look at things more from an ethno-national perspective than from that either of constitutional politics or law or international politics or law, to see things in those terms. These are discussions which have been raised about which there has been quite a lot of debate in some places. All I can say, as what I would regard as a matter of fact, is that in the process of dissolution of Yugoslavia, those interpretations of people regarding the inhabitants of a territory, i.e. one of the republics, is what has been accepted, broadly, in the debates between the Yugoslav states and by the international community and I may -- I think I will have opportunity to clarify some of this later. Going back specifically to the position of the JNA, it was charged with looking after the SFRY as a whole. It was not charged with taking responsibility for one particular group within the SFRY. So, at this point when the General indicates that for them the main aim, in practical terms, had come to be protecting and defending the Serb people outside Serbia and assembling the JNA within the borders of the future Yugoslavia, he was talking about creating something new, not preserving the old SFRY, but creating something new which would be a mini Yugoslavia or, in practical terms, as understood by many people, an expansion of the Republic of Serbia through the creation of a new federation. I hope that I did understand your question and that I have addressed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is envisioning the use of JNA troops to protect persons who are outside the territorial boundaries of Serbia at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people that he envisions that they have a responsibility to protect would be persons that are then defined in the, you say, 1974 constitution? That is, not just people within the geographic borders of Serbia, but persons located in other areas of Yugoslavia who are of Serbian descent. If I am wrong, tell me so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have thought that the appropriate interpretation of the role given in the 1974 constitution was to preserve the system which involved all the republics and all the communities of Yugoslavia rather than to take the role of protecting any one group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps just following on from what Her Honour said, there was a significant change, was there not, in the JNA by this time, i.e. had it moved from being the Federal Army charged with the responsibility of all of Yugoslavia, including Croatia, Slovenia and everything, and by what General Kadijevic is saying, it had shrunk back to what was to be the new Federation of Yugoslavia, namely, Serbia and Montenegro, and that the responsibility of the army would be to look after Serbs in that new federation, plus those outside of the new federation? Does that summarise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have gathered all of that and it does seem to summarise the situation. The JNA had responsibility for the whole of the territory of the SFRY and all the constituent elements, republics and peoples. In the situation of dissolution when, as the General says, there was no longer a real common Yugoslav state, no longer a real federation, the JNA was faced with a very difficult situation, I guess, and it fell back on aligning itself with a project -- for a state project based around the Serbian people throughout the territories of the SFRY, not in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was he writing this? What was the time that he was writing this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The time he was writing was -- the time he was writing about is the second half of 1991, throughout 1991, but particularly in the second half of 1991. The time he was writing it was in 1992 after he had left his position as Federal Secretary of Defence and as Head of the Army, and I think the book was eventually published in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. Now perhaps you would move on to look at page 72 for me, please, and perhaps, Dr. Gow, you might look at the exhibit first, page 72 first, before it is put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I would indicate that at this point, the point I am indicating now, the General identifies that there is a certain clear vision of a new Yugoslavia which had been taking shape, and that the JNA, therefore, moved to a conceptualisation and planning for its deployment in the context of creating that new Yugoslavia. He identifies the nature -- the existence of the JNA's transformation and its movement towards -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you just move it over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid that has taken it off the right-hand side of my screen.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I want you to see, but we were having difficulty on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Always it is too far over one side.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is fine by me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We can see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Secondly, I was saying, it indicates the JNA's national transformation with respect of the new Yugoslavia. Finally, I would indicate that again he identifies that the JNA had been carrying out its task of protecting the Serb people in Croatia under the rubric of preventing clashes between the peoples, preventing intercommunal violence, that is, in the course of 1991. The official JNA position had been that its deployment were only a matter of what it called "peacekeeping", of separating communities, of preventing intercommunal clashes, but he clearly indicates that in doing that it had seen its task of being that of defending the Serb people, but by this stage, in the second part of 1991, it could no longer carry out its task of protecting the Serb people in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it goes on over the page too to page 73.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I guess I just will not give up. What is the constitutional basis in any of the exhibits that we have that the nation of Serbia extended beyond the territorial borders reflected in Exhibit 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no clear constitutional basis that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is it reflected then that there is a larger nation of Serbia that goes beyond this territorial border in Exhibit 2, we will say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is reflected, I think, in the reality that there were Serbs living in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the "nations" being a word that would be "peoples" as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was again a degree of ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am trying to see if my fellow judges follow better than I do. I understand there was a belief that Serbia was more, yes, greater Serbia -- we have not heard that term used, but I know that is what you are talking about because I suppose we all read papers -- but where is it written that there was this belief that Serbia went beyond the territorial borders that we have seen? In the exhibits that we have -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that I have indicated anywhere that it is written, and I have not been trying to say that it was written. What I have been saying is that you had a set of states within a federation in which there was a degree of ambiguity and slight of hand in the way that certain terms were used. This reflected the fact that there was the Republic of Serbia as the titular state of the Serbs. But, as we saw in the discussion of the Serbian memorandum and the changes to the Serbian constitution in the late 1980s, that status was a matter of ambiguity and was questioned itself. As part of that discussion, I indicated that those who were drafting the memorandum expressed a concern, not only for the internal structures, the internal arrangements, for the Republic of Serbia, but also for what they termed the integrity of the Serbian people as a whole, i.e. the Serbian peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatia. The degree of ambiguity arises in part because, although Serbia was taken to be the titular state of the Serbs on one level, within the constitution of the SFRY, the Serbs as a whole were a state forming people. While ever you had the Federation, it did not matter whether the Serbs were in Croatia or in Bosnia or in Serbia because, as far as they were concerned about it at all, they would see themselves as being a state forming people. In the process of dissolution, the status of Serbs in Croatia and in Bosnia is brought into question, because within the SFRY they can say, "We are a state forming people". If Croatia and Bosnia are to become independent, there is a question mark against whether or not they will continue to be state forming people. In the Republic of Croatia, this was particularly pertinent. The 1974 constitution of the Republic of Croatia described the republic as the state of the Croatian and Serbian Peoples and others. The 1990 constitution adopted, after the nationalist government had come to power, made a slight change and said that Croatia was the state of the Croatian people and of the Serbs and of others. This was one of the questions which the Serbs in the areas I have mentioned this morning -- this is one of the things which concerned the Serbs in those areas which I mentioned because they saw their status being changed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought we had seen a constitution of Serbia that laid a claim to Serbs outside of the territorial boundary of Serbia and then you tell me there is ambiguity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, we did not see a constitution which said that; we saw the document of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences which indicated ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- a concern for it -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could follow up, the SANU memorandum had expressed in it, did it, Dr. Gow, this concept of the achievement of a greater Serbia, but perhaps not using those terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I missed the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am saying that the SANU memorandum had expressed in it this concept of greater Serbia without necessarily using those terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many people have interpreted the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences as being a blueprint, a document which was the basis for the idea of creating a great Serbia. I would have to say that that is not an idea which is explicitly expressed, as far as I can see, in the document, but the document does speak of the position of the integrity of the Serbian people as a whole. That could be interpreted as meaning providing a context in which all the Serbian people would come together, integrity meaning bringing them all within one context.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: At some point in this trial we will be focusing on a term that is referred to as "protective persons" coming from the Geneva Conventions. So the question that I am asking you really is not from a historical point of view, although this is very interesting, but I am really trying to get to that point. So, I do not want you to think that I am just asking questions to understand the historical development; I am very concerned about how Serbian people considered themselves, what state they considered themselves to belong to in various other republics, and whether there is any documentation that would indicate in writing that there was a connection between Serbia and Serbs in other republics. When I say "a connection", I am talking about an express national connection. That is really why I was focusing on that question. I am trying to relate the responsibility of the JNA forces at this time for Serbs in other republics. Really, that is what I am trying to focus on. Perhaps if I take a look -- it is an open ended question -- at the exhibits more carefully, maybe I can find the answer myself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to say that, whether it is for historical or military, political, international or any kind of background, I am only glad to help your Honours in any way that I can for whatever purpose. On this particular point, I think we need to separate two things. The first is that the memorandum in the terms you were just expressing is in itself an expression of this idea of bringing Serbian peoples together, albeit in a non -- not explicitly determined way. None of the constitutional provisions or, indeed, any of the constitutional documents to which we have made reference so far give any indication of a responsibility of the Republic of Serbia or of the JNA for Serbian peoples specifically outside the Republic of Serbia. So, I think that would clarify the point in your mind. So the JNA had, in the action that it was taking to protect the Serbian people, the JNA was not acting on any constitutional basis at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. That was my question. You can articulate my question better than I can. We will stand in recess for lunch until 2.30. (1.05 p.m.) (Luncheon Adjournment) (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you proceed, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, before the luncheon adjournment, we were looking, in particular, at Exhibit 30 which is the book written by General Kadijevic. I had shown to you pages 61 and 72 of the book. There was one final page I wanted to take you to, namely, page 73. Would you now look at that page, please, page 73? In connection with that page, can you take us to the relevant part in relation to the role, the changing role, of the JNA following the break up or during the course of the break up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can, I will draw your attention to this first full paragraph in which the General talks about the changed situation in which he identifies the aim to create a new Yugoslavia made up of nations which so desired. In this context, "nations", I suspect, I would think, has been used in the sense of an ethno-national nation, i.e. an ethno-national group wherever it is found as distinct from a people inhabiting a territory -- the kind of distinction we were talking about in the morning session. Although he expresses the desire to do this peacefully and equitably, it is clear that he is talking about the whole situation as a war and, as far as he is talking about those nations which wish to remain part of this new Yugoslavia, it would be fair to say that Slovenia and the Slovenes and the Croats in Croatia had already indicated they did not want to be part of this new Yugoslavia. Macedonia had indicated that it no longer wished to be part of it and that although at the time he is describing in his writing the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina had not been made clear in a formal way, it was certainly the case that the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina, President Itzebegovic, had said that although he wished to find a solution, the best solution for both his Muslim population and for Bosnia and Herzegovina within some kind of Yugoslav arrangement, he would not allow it to remain in a federation which would be, effectively, a greater Serbia. In a sense, what I am making clear here is that when the General says those nations which -- talks about the nations who did not wish to remain part of this new Yugoslavia and, conversely, those who did, he is, effectively, talking about the Serbs who wish to remain part of it and the others who do not. I would go on to say that he identifies that in this phase of the war, the objective of the JNA was to protect the Serb people in Croatia in such a way that all the areas, all regions, with a majority Serb population would be completely freed from the presence of the Croatian Army and the Croatian authorities before pulling the JNA out of Croatia. I think this would indicate that the aim was, as far as we were discussing the possible borders of this new mini Yugoslavia this morning, one of the first points in which we can begin to identify borders is that it would be around the areas designated as being Serbian majority areas or with a significant Serbian population in Croatia, and the objective of the JNA was to establish the borders of the new entity based around those populations. I would also point out that in the book the General identifies two phases of operations in Croatia. The first phase would be to secure the territories with Serbian populations; the second phase would have been to move on to try to topple the Croatian government. I think that second phase in the objective was abandoned well before the end of 19 -- before the end of 1991. If you move down, you will see that the General identifies the objective as being total defeat of the Croatian army, if they were able to do, and certainly to fulfil the main goal, the main minimum goals and, in doing so, there would be full co-ordination with Serbian insurgents in the Serbian Krajina, that is, in the region of Krajina we talked about this morning, and in the other regions which were designated to be part of the declared autonomous regions. At that same time, he also indicates there was awareness of the potential role for the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that this would be instrumental and vital to the future of this project as it was to develop in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Could you put that back? In the first complete paragraph, the third last line reads " ... of Croatia, to pull the JNA out of Croatia". That does not mean Croatia as comprised at any time really; it means that part of Croatia which was inhabited by Croats, is that so? It is a curious use of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it can be interpreted in that way, and the intention is to convey the sense that Croatia for this purpose would be Croatia without the areas, either with Serbian majority populations or otherwise under Serbian control. I would point out also that there was also the fact, as it developed at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, in fact, was that the JNA decided technically to withdraw from Croatia, so that means, first, it withdrew from the non-Serbian controlled areas in Croatia, but then also it withdrew elements of its forces from the areas under Serbian control, but redesignated them as a local militia force for the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina. So, in one sense, it left the forces behind, but in another it would say technically that it withdrew some of them and it withdrew them as the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, there is, obviously, a contradiction between protecting the Serb people in Croatia -- two lines above -- and pulling the JNA out of Croatia. They are talking of doing the two things at the same time and he is using Croatia in different senses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is quite possible to read it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was trying to indicate that, as a matter of fact, at the end of 1991 ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I realise that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the JNA said that it was withdrawing from Croatia and formally there was no JNA presence left, although there was a de facto JNA presence which was then designated the armed forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. So, it would say technically it had withdrawn, de facto the presence remained. It is a slightly ambiguous situation. I think you are quite right to identify the ambiguity within the phrasing there because I believe you are right to identify the second use of Croatia does exclude the territories under Serbian control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I have a question to address to you. The General here speaks of Serbian Krajina. Is Krajina an amorphous area or a properly demarcated area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That may depend on which Krajina you are talking about. It was a properly demarcated the Vojna Krajina, to which I made reference this morning, the historical area within the Hapsburg Empire, was a properly demarcated area. The term has been used loosely since then to refer to the territories either side of the border between Bosnia and Croatia in that area in north western Bosnia, around the north western corner of Bosnia and in the Dalmatian hinterland. So, for example, you have an area in north western Bosnia which is also sometimes referred to as Krajina. In terms of the declaration of the Republic of Serbian Krajina or, prior to that, the Serbian autonomous region of Krajina, it was designated to include particular municipalities within the Republic of Croatia and, therefore, was given in some areas certainly a particular designation, although when it became the Republic of Serbian Krajina, it was also to include territories in Eastern Slovenia which were not part of the conventional use of the term to describe the Dalmatian hinterland areas on the border with Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you have finished with that page, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may check? I cannot remember any more. If I may just point out at this stage for future reference -- I may want to come back to this page -- simply the General identifies the organisation of the JNA, and at this point here identifies the main directions of lines of attack for the JNA forces operating in Croatia and out of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Shall I indicate it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It still needs to go over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: There is a technical difficulty. Apparently, your screen operates differently from mine and, I think, ours. For instance, at the moment one edge, we have lost a lot of the print.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What we need to achieve, your Honour, is the one that can best be read by your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you now see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think we are finished with that exhibit now anyway, so if that can be handed back.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: After all that effort!

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, notwithstanding the fact that historically and constitutionally the JNA was a force in respect of all of the republics and all of the nations and nationalities of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was there any one particular ethnic group that historically had a more dominant position, if I could call it that, in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the officer corps of the JNA, ethnic Serbs were a predominant group forming about 60 per cent of the total of the officer corps, although, if you recall from some of the information we looked at in testimony yesterday afternoon, the Serbs formed only around 34 to 36 per cent of the population as a whole. So, you see, there was a disproportionate representation of Serbs within the officer corps. In part, I think, this can be explained as a matter of tradition and, in particular, because the JNA was the successor of the partisan movement, and that Serbs from Croatia and Bosnia, in particular, had been the core of the partisan movement in the early years of the Second World War; so this gave rise to tradition, very common within military sociology of military families bequeathing military families bequeathing military families, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did this dominant Serbian position in the JNA develop during the early part of the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of the 1990s, the JNA, as it came into its final phase as the JNA, became increasingly dominated by Serbian elements. This would be both at the conscript kada level and at the regular level within the officer corps as, on the one side, the non-Serbs increasingly left service and, on the other side, there was an increasing sense of a Serbian identity emerging, I think, among elements of the JNA officer corps, although this was a matter of some -- it was a process which was taking place and there was a tension between those who had what I would describe as a Yugoslav orientation and those who were clearly shaping, adapting to the future of a Serbian orientation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was this Serbian orientation of the JNA evidenced in April and May 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That orientation began to be demonstrated in the spring of 1991 in Croatia and I think continued to be demonstrated in the course of that year as the JNA began to deploy troops in areas of Croatia with significant Serbian populations under their technical remit of preventing intercommunal clashes but, as we saw from General Kadijevic's book, with the real intention of what it described as protecting the Serbian people, that is, beginning to deploy in a way which was consistent with giving assistance to Serbian groups within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time -- we are speaking April/May 1991 -- what was the attitude of the command of the JNA towards the formal constitutional dictates of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was some dispute within the high levels of the JNA at this time. There was broadly agreement about the crisis situation. According to General Kadijevic and some other sources, there was a plan in the spring of 1991 to try to declare a state of emergency to prevent those things which would happen afterwards. There was a difference of opinion as reported in some, at least apparently, according to some reports that appeared of leaked conversations between General Kadijevic, as the Federal Secretary of Defence, and General Adzic, his Chief of Staff. General Adzic seemed to favour direct action irrespective of constitutional requirements; whereas General Kadijevic seemed to be attached to the idea that the JNA had a constitutional role and had to behave constitutionally. This is a somewhat ambiguous situation again because General Kadijevic himself was doing things which might be interpreted as unconstitutionally at the same time as he had reservations about behaving in a constitutional manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would ask if you could, please, turn on your video monitor and I would then ask that a video representing Exhibit 31 be played for you, please, the first introduction segment of that video, if that could please be played first?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you play it, I presume you are going to offer it and there is no objection to 31 -- is it 31, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is going to be Exhibit 31, yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is on list of exhibits for identification purposes as 31?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I can indicate, it is the "Death of Yugoslavia" series. It is just some short portions from it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Let us see 31 then. 31 has various portions to it. I guess it is tape 1 now that we are going to see?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is just the introduction to identify the video. Then I will ask for the playing of part 1. The parts are very short; they are matters of seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. (The video was played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just looking at that short introduction piece, Dr. Gow, are you aware of who prepared -- did your Honours see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have a problem here, your Honour. We did not see anything on our screens.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did you turn on the video monitor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I see. We were on the computer. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps it might be played again? Your Honour, I would ask for it to be played again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could that be wound back and then the introduction part played again, please? (The video was again played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, just looking at that short video segment there, are you aware, firstly, of the name of the production?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The production was the "Death of Yugoslavia".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was responsible for it? Who produced it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was produced by Brian Lapping Associates in London for the BBC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any involvement yourself closely in this production?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was one of the consultants involved in discussing and preparing the material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you during the course of your evidence refer to various excerpts from this series?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I might tender that, your Honours, as Exhibit 31 and the various parts that we now go to, if they can be numbered parts 1, 2, 3 and so forth of Exhibit 31 -- if that is acceptable to your Honours?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have listed Exhibit 31. Then you have various tapes, programme 2, for example, tape 1, programme 3, and then you have the minute, seconds, under that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, if they could be just referred to as parts of Exhibit 31, I think, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You want to play them continuously?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, they come at different pieces of the evidence. I do not think it would be too awkward that way. If they are all played together, then we will lose the sequence of them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have seen these exhibits, Mr. Wladimiroff; do you have any objection to 31, any of the tapes that are listed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have no objection to showing it to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, very good. Then 31 will come in and you will tell us whether we are watching tape 1 or tape 1, programme 2, 3 etc. or do you want me to make them 31(a) for tape 1, 31(b) for tape 1, programme 3? That is the way I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: However your Honour feels .....

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are trying to determine whether what you have offered is one continuous tape that will just shows us tape 1, programme 2, and then it would go to on tape 1, programme 3, is that the way it is being offered?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What has happened is there is one tape with the various parts on it which we can play each part, but it is one actual cassette tape.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Then it will come in then as one exhibit, 31. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): I would ask that part 1 be played and perhaps what I will do, Dr. Gow, is would you just watch through and then we will play it again and as we go back through it I will get you to explain the various part as we go through, if you would not mind. So could part 1 of Exhibit 31 now be played? (Part 1 of Exhibit 31 was played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps the volume might be raised a little bit? Perhaps, just before we replay that, can you tell us, Dr. Gow, what was that clip about, what was that film about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The extract was mostly based around a secret film taken of an emergency meeting of the collective federal presidency in March 1991. That emergency meeting was called at the request of the Minister of Defence, General Kadijevic, to discuss the situation in Yugoslavia. The secret film of the meeting was taken by military intelligence. It was made as a record of a meeting in which the army was attempting to persuade the collective federal presidency to declare a state of emergency throughout the territories of the SFRY in order, in the General's terms, to prevent the impending break up of the federation. It was a meeting in which, as you could see, there was some difficulty; it was a meeting, the outcome of which was not that desired by the General. It was a meeting which for certain aspects the General had been co-ordinating with one of the men you saw in the film, Borisav Jovic, who was the Serbian representative to the collective presidency, in order to create the conditions for this state of emergency. But the presidency, as a whole, would not vote for it. It was split 4:4 and, therefore, the state of emergency was not declared. The final section of the film that you saw, saw Jovic and Admiral Branko Mamula, who was Kadijevic's predecessor as Federal Secretary for Defence and went on to be Kadijevic's adviser, indicating that Kadijevic for certain reservations had not gone ahead and declared a state of emergency in spite of the decision. I would say that that decision -- Kadijevic took that decision largely because he could not bring himself to act outside without a specific order from the collective federal presidency. Jovic seems to have expected that he would act anyway, and at one stage he threatened that he would in the course of the scene you saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so you can point out the characters to us, I know they were named, but so the characters could be pointed out, could we play it again and at some segments I will stop, ask that the film be stopped. So could it be played again, please? (The video was again played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just stopping there for a moment, this is the General Kadijevic whose book has been tendered as Exhibit 30?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was 19 but .....

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue on, please. Just stop for a moment, please. Who is this gentleman that you just saw there before the -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is Vasil Tupurkovski who was the Macedonian representative to the collective federal presidency, and who was one of the people in attendance at that meeting of the collective federal presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could it be played on now? Just stopping for a moment, please, who is this gentleman we now see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Stipe Mesic who was the Croatian representative to the collective federal presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the gentleman that was stopped from becoming the President of the presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was; at this stage he was in the position to become President of the presidency two months later in May, and it was his appointment which was blocked on 15th May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that could be played on, please? Continue. Just stopping there for a moment, please, can you assist us with what is meant by having "no civilian commander"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man who is speaking, and you just began to see his face, was Borislav Jovic who was the Serbian representative to the collective federal presidency, and he is indicating that in a situation where the collective federal presidency had not agreed to declare the state of emergency, then he thought that Kadijevic should say there is no civilian commander, therefore, would declare a state of emergency anyway. He then goes on to point out that, among other things, Kadijevic was worried that this would be seen as a military coup.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue on. Just stopping there for a moment, please. Who is this gentleman that we see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Admiral Branko Mamula who I already said was previously Federal Secretary of Defence before Kadijevic and was acting as an adviser to Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue on. Thank you. Dr. Gow, now turning to the question of the involvement of the Serbs in the JNA during the period of the armed conflict, what happened to the process of Serb domination of the JNA after the outbreak of hostilities in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the outbreak of hostilities in 1991, the JNA -- the gradual process of transformation which had already begun in the JNA was increased greatly and, for the most part, non-Serbs left the JNA and it was by the end of 1991, certainly by the early part of 1992, that the JNA had been transformed from a largely multi-ethnic armed force comprised of people from all the territories of the SFRY into a largely Serbian force both in the officer corps and in the rank and file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with that, Dr. Gow, would you, please, look at the document that you are now shown?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, on what do you base that, that opinion, that the JNA had been transformed from a multinational force to a predominantly Serbian force by the time of the outbreak of hostilities in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not hear the last part of the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what do you base that opinion, the opinion that you just gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I base the opinion on information published and reported and I believe will be coming to show some of that evidence on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have a document, your Honour, which will follow this one, I think. It might assist your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will just sit back and listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry. (To the witness): Perhaps just looking at the document that I now show you, though, Dr. Gow, and can you tell me what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a schedule showing the share of particular ethnic groups within the JNA officer corps as a whole, and indicating the specific numbers of each ethnic grouping at the ranks of General Colonel and Lieutenant Colonel in the JNA for figures published in April 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who prepared this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This schedule was prepared at my direction by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that schedule, if your Honours please. That is No. 32.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 32, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 32 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After it has been marked, might it be returned to the witness, please? Can that be placed on the overhead projector and, Dr. Gow, could you explain to us the numbers that are written there and the significance of them, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first of the tables shown indicating national composition of the officer corps as a whole, you will see the first -- you have the list of the different ethno-national groupings on the left-hand side. The first column indicates the percentage share of that particular group in the officer corps as a whole, and the second column indicates the percentage share of the Yugoslav population as a whole. This goes towards confirming something that I already said in an earlier part of the testimony, for example, that around 60 per cent of the officer corps were Serbs as against only 36 per cent of the population as a whole; conversely, you can see that whereas, for example, Slovenes comprised 7.8 per cent of the population as a whole, they comprised only 2.8 per cent of the officer corps. It is simply an indication of the degree to which Serbs were the predominant group within the officer corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell us the date that this relates to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information is derived from a then Slovenian language Yugoslav Defence publication, Revija Obramba, in April 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bottom schedule? Is that visible to your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second of the tables indicates the actual numbers for each ethno-national grouping at the various ranks displayed across the top, so for General, for Colonel and for Lieutenant Colonel. Then you will see that although there may be what I would identify as a broad attempt to preserve as far as possible proportionality in the higher ranks at General, at the General level, you will see at the level of Colonel and Lieutenant Colonel, the number of Serbs becomes out of proportion again with that of the other groupings. There is a note attached to the bottom which is that many of those who identified themselves as Yugoslav were also, could also possibly be identified as Serbs in certain situations. They were of Serbian origin but chose to designate themselves as Yugoslav, but by no means exclusively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would ask you to look at the next document that I show you and perhaps that document could be returned to the Registrar? Her Honour Judge MacDonald asked you a moment ago if you had a source for that information. Can you tell us what the document is that I have just handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is the cover of Revija Obramba for April 1991, the edition of the volume in which the information we just saw on the previous schedule, from where the information was derived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell us what that publication is, please, if you would?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a Slovenian language defence publication in the SFRY; the title means "Defence review".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you regard that as a reliable source of information in connection with your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
