utterances.text: I do regard it as a reliable source and would add that the particular information involved, the article in which it appears, was produced by a man which was working in the Defence staff in Belgrade and was produced from authoritative Ministry of Defence sources. That is what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, as a result of that particular publication, did you yourself in one of your own articles make reference to the material contained in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and the tables that we saw before the schedules prepared in the Office of the Prosecutor were broadly similar to the tables in the article "Deconstructing Yugoslavia" which appeared in the journal "Survival" in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The article "Deconstructing Yugoslavia" is your article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my article, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender those documents, if your Honour please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 33?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 33 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once the document has been exhibited, could it be handed back to the witness? In order to complete the answer that you gave to Judge McDonald in relation to its source, could you display just the front cover of that on the overhead projector and then show the sources contained in the article which, I believe, appears in the Serbo-Croat or the Serbian language; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is in the Slovene language. The information appeared in a series of bar graph charts, as indicated. I do not think you are going to be able to see as presented here the actual percentages and figures of which I spoke which were indicated at the bottom of the bar graphs as you move along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, what happened you interpolated that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the purpose of the article and then for the purpose of the schedule for the Office of the Prosecutor, I had that information converted into the table we saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, perhaps, just show us the first section of your publication. That is your article and I think you have also reproduced in your article the same schedule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I reproduce the same information in the schedule and it was a version of that table which was taken for use by Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow, what impact did the dissolution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the armed conflict in 1991 and 1992 have on the ethnic composition of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe this will also go partly in answer to Judge MacDonald's earlier question. I began to indicate that the structure, the ethnic composition, ethnic structure, of the JNA changed radically in the course of the armed conflict after June 1991, so that by the spring of 1992, whereas there had been an army in which around 40 per cent of the total officer and rank and file, a little over 40 per cent, were Serbian, by the spring of 1992 that figure had risen to somewhere around or in excess of 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at the exhibit, the document, I will now show you? (Handed) Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a bar graph representation to indicate the change in the share of Serbs and non-Serbs in the Yugoslav Army between June 1991 and March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who prepared the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document was prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor at my direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the source of the information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information was derived from press reports of Belgrade Ministry of Defence statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour. It is document No. 34.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 34?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 34 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once that is marked, could it then be displayed on the overhead projector? (To the witness): Dr. Gow, just looking at this, I think it maybe useful to show it -- no, I think we can see it, can we see it all in one? Perhaps I might ask you to go through it and explain it. This document relates to what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We cannot see the percentage numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps if we deal with it in two parts, that is best. Tell us what it is, describe it for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a bar graph representation of the percentage share of conscripts within the JNA at the stage, at the two different stages. Before June 1991, this is based on an estimate that the number of conscripts of each group within the JNA would be proportional with the share of the total population of the SFRY. So, if there were 36 per cent of Serbs within the SFRY between the ages of 18 and 24, then approximately 36 per cent of JNA conscript kada would be Serbs. The table indicates that there were, therefore, around 36 per cent of Serbs at that stage and a figure, conversely, approaching 64 per cent of non-Serbs. The white column indicates Serbs, the darker column indicates non-Serbs. You will see the percentage shares marked on the scale to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just to summarise that, the percentage of Serb composition which is represented by the white block was approximately in accord -- this is of the conscripts -- with their percentage of the population preJune 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After June 1991, could you then show us the next stage? This is March 1992, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are figures for March 1992 which were reported in March 1992, and you will see the white block, the share of Serbs within the army has risen to the point of 90 per cent and that, conversely, the proportion of non-Serbs has fallen to 10 per cent. Of that 10 per cent which constituted 11,000 people, 6,500 were Montenegrins who throughout, certainly for the purposes of discussing the army, are conventionally regarded as being Serbs without being Serbian; I am not quite sure to what extent it is always accurate, always the best thing to do to regard it that way, but certainly conventionally. So, within that 10 per cent, perhaps 5 per cent, slightly over 5 per cent, would be Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a consequence of these dramatic changes to the composition of both the officer corps which we saw earlier and of the ethnic composition of the conscripts of the JNA, by this time March 1992, is it fair to say that it had, essentially, become a Serbian military force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would think it is certainly fair to say that both in terms of its composition and, broadly, the purpose for which it was being used, by this time it had become a military force, a Serbian military force, although that was not its official designation. Its official designation at this stage was still Yugoslav People's Army, but that was to be changed in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were some of the main players that led the campaign inside the JNA for its Serbian reorientation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I indicated already that there was some tension within the JNA leadership and that some people, for example, General Kadijevic may have had a slightly more conservative and proYugoslav view, other people have been reported as having slightly more proSerbian views and among those certainly a member of the Air Force General staff, General Bozidar Stevanovic, has been reported as being significant in leading a campaign from within the armed forces to make the armed forces more Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Stevanovic do in this process of reorientating the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stevanovic who had actually put in his resignation in the summer of 1991 and, quite exceptionally, had the resignation recalled, both according to reports gave instructions to elements of the Air Force military intelligence to prepare information on other people within the JNA leadership, information which would then be used in part of two phases of purging JNA Generals in the spring of 1992. So that where of the 150 Generals that there had been in the JNA as a whole, the JNA comprises ground forces, Air Forces and Navy, and before June 1991 there had been 150 Generals, after March 1992 only 28 of those who had been serving in June continued to be with the JNA, either because they had left to go because they wanted to be no part of what was happening, or to join one of the other armed forces, or because in the case of 58 of them, they had been either moved out or moved into early retirement, and the work of Stevanovic was reported, and the people working for him was reported as being significant in making that happen. I would also point out that Stevanovic also, another line of activity was reported as having significant links with certain paramilitary leaders who would go to Air Force posts to 252 at Batajnica where Stevanovic would enter into discussions and was reported as making services available to them, such as provision of helicopters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the relationship of these paramilitary units were with the JNA? At this time now, I am talking mid 1991 onwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a number of paramilitary groups which operated on the territories of Croatia and then on Bosnia and Herzegovina. For the most part, these acted in co-operation with the JNA. They served different purposes. Some of them were more significant than others. The most significant ones served two purposes: First, they had a Serbian designation. This meant that some people who would be prepared to go to fight for a Serbian but not a Yugoslav cause would be prepared to join these groups. Many people had a lack of faith in the Yugoslav People's Army, and that it would be serving the interests of the Serbian people, so one point was that it would be a focal point for those who would be prepared to fight for a Serbian cause at a time when many Serbs were deserting from the JNA. The second point was that the JNA anyway with its multi-ethnic and even when it became a more purely Serbian conscript kada was not in a position to launch significant ground operations using infantry. Therefore, whilst the JNA was prepared to use its artillery in operations, it relied on paramilitary groups to go into built up areas and to act as a substitute infantry. In these ways, the paramilitary groups and the JNA were co-operating and, broadly, paramilitary groups were operating under the command and framework of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify some of these particular paramilitary groups or units by name and the people responsible for leading them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a number of groups. There was the Serbian Volunteer Guard led by Zeljko Raznjatovic, known commonly as "Arkan". There were different groups such as the White Eagles, Beli Orli, and the Chetniks, groups which were led by people such as Vojislav Seselj and Dragoslav Bokan and Mirko Jovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any assistance given to these particular paramilitary groups by the Yugoslav Air Force particularly in the period 1991/92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly some assistance was reported particularly focused around General Stevanovic and the Air Force base at Batjanica. Supplies were said to be given to paramilitaries at those bases and also there were reports that, for example, Seselj made use of helicopters from the JNA base there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a consequence -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just clarify, that is according to Seselj himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was in Bosnia? Was there involvement of the Air Force in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same groups operated in Croatia and in Bosnia, and there was a degree of Air Force support for those groups, as for the JNA as a whole. Certainly in the early stages of the war in Bosnia, as during the war in Croatia, the Air Force also maintained, among other things, an air bridge between the eastern -- between the territory of Serbia in the eastern part of Bosnia and the western parts of Bosnia under Serb control and the Serb controlled areas in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this assistance rendered by the Yugoslav Air Force to the paramilitaries continue on through the period of 1992 or the year of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any international reaction to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an international reaction specifically to the use and the potential use of the Air Force in Bosnia and Herzegovina which was the declaration of an air exclusion zone, no fly zone, over Bosnia and Herzegovina which was declared, I think, under UN Security Council Resolution 781.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just ask you to look at this document, please. (Handed) Is that the United Nations Resolution 781?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is indeed the Resolution to which I have just made reference dated 9th October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there objection to 35? Security Council Resolution 781, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 35 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps the document might be handed back to the witness you might just indicate, if you would, Dr. Gow, where this is referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I might indicate?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just where the Resolution relating to this -- perhaps just show the first page so that we can may identify it, the Resolution, and then just go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I point to operative paragraph (1) of the Resolution in which this Security Council indicates that it has decided to establish a ban on military flights in the air space of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the exception of flights relating to United Nations activities or all flights approved by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the next document that is shown to you, please? What is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is a report of the Secretary General of the United Nations pursuant to Security Council Resolution 871, 1993, and it is the report with the reference S/1994/300, dated 16th March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I tender the Security General's report.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 36?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 36 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once the document is marked, could you please hand it back to Dr. Gow? (To the witness): Dr. Gow, going to page 8 of the Secretary General's report at paragraph 23, if you would, please? By reference to that particular part of the Secretary General's report, is that a reference to the establishment of this no fly zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, and I would point out that this particular Secretary General's report as a whole is a report, an overall report, on the UN operations with regard to former Yugoslavia, and this particular section relates to the no fly zone under Security Council Resolution 781. Other parts, of course, refer to other aspects of the UN operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you look now, please, at the next document which is shown to you. That one may be returned to the Registrar. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, would you mind if I do this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the document goes, can I also point out that it makes reference to the Resolution 781 and implementation of it and also notes, if you will see in paragraph 24, that between October 1992 and March 1993, it records 540 violations of the ban on military flights which had been ordered under Resolution 781, although a small number of those were by Croatian forces, not by Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the next document you are shown? Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is, I think, taken as an extract from the volume Yugoslavia through Documents edited by Snezana Trifunovska, to which reference has already been made, and this particular extract relates to a statement of the government of Yugoslavia on 12th May 1992. In this case the government of Yugoslavia would refer to the declared government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that document, if your Honour pleases, document No. 37. Once it is tendered could it be handed back?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 37 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just going to the second page -- I think it is probably the best reference -- read the document first, though, would you, please? Perhaps that could be highlighted or enlarged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I draw your attention to the second paragraph in which this statement recalls that the Yugoslav presidency, that is, Serbia and Montenegro, has decided to withdraw the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina and that it speaks about completing this process within 10 days, although it should also be said that originally it indicated that the force would be withdrawn by 19th May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us the significance -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What was the date on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 12th May 1992. If you wish, I will just show you the first page -- sorry, it was published in the Yugoslav publication, Review of International Affairs, 12th May. It relates to the decision on 4th May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the significance of this -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I am just -- no, sorry, I take that back. The statement is for 12th May and it was published in the Review of International Affairs, by the look of it, in the summer, June or July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the significance of this decision with relation to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The significance of the decision to withdraw the JNA, at least in a formal sense, is that the leaders of the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, Serbia and Montenegro, particularly the leaders of Serbia, saw that the continuing presence of the JNA on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period of armed conflict in which those forces were engaged would lead to an adverse international assessment. This had all been indicated by discussion of possibly -- by a request of the Security Council to withdraw the JNA and also by the indication that a sanctions regime might be imposed against Serbia and Montenegro if the JNA were not to be withdrawn. Therefore, the significance is that the Yugoslav government was attempting, that is, the government of Serbia and Montenegro, was attempting to send the message that it would withdraw its forces from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, thank you. I am just returning for a moment to the involvement of the paramilitaries with the JNA. You mentioned earlier in your evidence that there was a lack of confidence in the loyalty of the Serbs in the JNA. Can you tell us why there was this lack of confidence, why was there this concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would judge that there was a lack of confidence in the JNA, in part, because throughout the war in Croatia the Yugoslav Army had spent a lot of the time not obviously fighting for the Serbian or, rather, not fighting on the Serbian side in open terms, as we made reference to the extract from General Kadijevic's book earlier. The General indicated that they were operating within the rubric of separating the communities and, therefore, the real objective of protecting the Serbian people could not be stated. The inability to state a clear objective because of the situation and the need to prevent it from becoming categorically clear in stated terms what the JNA was doing meant that many people regarded it as an inefficient, inadequate force looking at what was happening in Croatia, and also made the judgment that, perhaps, it had too much of a Yugoslav orientation and not enough of a Serbian orientation. This goes to some of the discussion we already had about moves, pressures, on the JNA both from without and from within the force.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: At this time, what was the per cent again of Serbians in the JNA, conscripts as opposed to officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of this statement that we are discussing and the decision, by this time the percentage share of Serbs within the JNA was in excess of 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would now ask if part 2 of Exhibit 31, the video part 2, could be played. If your Honours could turn on the video monitor and, hopefully, we can all see it together then.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Part 2 will be tape 1, programme 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is just Exhibit 31, it is the one tape, your Honour, it is the second part of part 2. There is a whole series of interviews that will then follow all as part 2.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see. Programme 3, I guess you call the second part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, if you go down the page, part 2, there is a series of interviews under the heading "part 2" where it says Vojislav Seselj, Bokan and then there is a report on ethnic cleansing. All of that represents part of part 2.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is part 2. I am really trying to decide for the record. Part 2 of ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of Exhibit 31.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- Exhibit 31, tape 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not think it refers to the tapes. The tapes, if I can explain ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The tape is called "Death of Yugoslavia" and you have part 1, you have played at least a portion of part 1. Now you are going to play a portion of part 2 which, I gather, will begin with what you have listed on your exhibit list as tape 1, programme 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. There are a number of tapes and a number of programmes. This merely identifies where they come out of a five part series of a BBC production. For the purposes of these proceedings, your Honours, this merely indicates from where they have been extracted and it assists in working out where they have come from, but the part, part 2, will all be together. It will all be just one section. It is merely there to assist in locating from where the series had been taken. It is a whole series of very short excerpts, but it will all be part 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: It is a rerecording.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is recording, rerecording.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There were five parts, I gather?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is a five part series.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is a five part series. What we are now going to see is the beginning of part 2, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honours, you are not. Part 2 is our designation. That is what we have called it for the purposes of these proceedings. We called it part 2, part 3 and part 4, but there the programme itself is divided into five parts.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You know what you have to do? It is very simple. You have an exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will you please point to where on your exhibit list you are getting ready to play? I gather you are getting ready to play what you have listed as tape 1, programme 3; if not, why did you list it as the second one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am being told a number of things at the Bar table here and none of them seem to be making any sense to me, so if I may consult, your Honours? Does your Honour have this document here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have it and I can read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The highlighted -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You tell me what is coming next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Part 2. If your Honours see highlighted part 2, part 2 is in highlighted. That is our designation and has nothing to do with the series. It is a number we have given it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am just asking you what you are going to play. You refer on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am going to play all of part 2, every one that is marked part 2 and highlighted.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. So you will begin with what is listed as part 2 and is list as tape 1, programme 3, interview with V-O-J-I-S-L-A-V S-E-S-E-L-J.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it will continue on, to the next part 2 and to the next part 2, and then there won’t be reference to part 4 will be a later tape.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you are only going to play three of the part tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I am going to play all of them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All four, OK, very good. We have not seen, I gather, tape 1, programme 3, because that is highlighted part 3 and that is going to come after part 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tape 1, programme 3, your Honour, has not been -- that part out of that has not been played yet.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Do you have any objection? 31 is all in, Mr. Wladimiroff, because you do not have an objection to any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, we have no objections.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: For the record then, we will begin to hear and see part 2 which is listed as tape 1, programme 3, on your exhibits list; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, part 2, your Honour, the reference, it is part 2 of the Exhibit 31. If it could be played, your Honour, I think it is the best way to identify it. (Part 2 of Exhibit 31 was played) Dr. Gow, before we go back and ask that to be played and stopped at various portions of it, can you tell us in an overview sense what those series of clips related to and the time of them, the relevant period in terms of what they were referring to? There were two separate periods, I know, there was period later, but the period that was basically being referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The set of extracts of interviews referred to the action of certain paramilitary groups, primarily those organised by Vojislav Seselj of the Serbian Radical Party, the Chetniks operating, first of all, in the warring Croatia in Eastern Slavonia, around Vukovar, and later in Bosnia, throughout the set of extracts indicates the way in which from the first extract showed General Zivota Panic, who was commander of the 1st military district at the time of the Vukovar campaign and was later to be Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav Army, indicating that the Army itself used its artillery and would not become engaged in fighting in urban areas. I already made reference to this situation in which, without a suitable infantry because of the problems with the conscript kada, the Army turned to the paramilitary groups and made use of them. The extracts also indicate the way in which, according to Seselj, the Serbian Security Service was involved in giving assistance, and the way in which elements from the Yugoslav Army would co-operate with his forces. This series of extracts, I think, gives you some indication of the way in which the paramilitary groups were operating, and the way they were co-operating with official bodies of the Republic of Serbia, in particular, the insertion of President Milosovic saying that all this is ridiculous, it is there because it is part of the flow of clip and is to be contrasted with the claims being made by Seselj in the interviews being shown. If I may before we move on may be try to help your Honour, Judge MacDonald, to explain the way in which these are being presented, given the difficulty that there was before we showed the video. The series "Death of Yugoslavia" has five parts. It will eventually have a sixth part. All five programmes are referred to in the list as programme 1, programme 2, programme 3, usually in the second column, indicates from which programme a particular extract was taken, and it also gives the timing of the point on the tape at which it appears. The extracts from different programmes sometimes appear as packages and, for the purposes of the evidence, I think, may be rather than being described as part 1 and part 2, could be described as reference 1 and reference 2 to the individual tape of extracts which is being used for the purpose of giving evidence and which I believe is going to be, when we have finished using it, handed over as an exhibit. I hope you do not mind me trying to help clarify that and I hope I have clarified it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The reason it is important is that some people may want to look at this. I suppose this is a record and it needs to be clear. What is the date on these parts, part 2? Part 1 was, of course, in the spring of 1991. What is the date for part 2, do you know, Mr. Niemann? Can you answer that for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think I would rather the assistance of Dr. Gow, your Honour, in terms of identifying those particular dates. I know the first one is OK, but in relation to the interview with Seselj, I may get him to indicate the approximate period, if I could, when we go through it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That would help, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interview itself was made in the course of making the five-part -- the five programmes for "Death of Yugoslavia" and was made in the course of 1994 or 1995. I cannot tell you exactly on which date the interview was made, but I think it is in the early part of 1995. The incidents to which Seselj is making reference are to incidents in Croatia in 1991 and to Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could see the tape, I think it is probably easier in context of each segment. I would ask that the tape be stopped at various portions throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have one short question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We have heard of conscripts and we have heard of officers. What surprises me is that I have heard nothing about non-commissioned officers, the Corporals, the Sergeants, the people who really make the army run. They are not conscripts, I assume. They are regulars. What was their nationality or are they included in the list of officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are not included in the list of officers. Conventionally, the non-commissioned officers were taken from the conscript kada. In the course of the 1980s, the Yugoslav People's Army moved towards a system in which some non-commissioned officers were on a contract basis, that is, volunteer non-commissioned officers. The total, before I gave an indication that about 60 per cent of the officer corps were of Serbian origin, the similar figure, if you take the whole of the volunteer kada on figures that I had from around 1988 -- I do not remember exactly any more -- were approximately 44 per cent, but I do not remember the figure exactly any more. But sometime in the mid/late 1980s after the system of contractualisation was introduced, the figure for the total volunteer element, that is, officers and non-commissioned officers was in the region of, as I recall, 44 per cent, but I make clear ---

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that I am not absolutely certain about that any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, might that be played again and we will go through it and identify the various parts of it. (The video was again played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just stopping there, could we stop there for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Stop the tape. I think he thinks that we want it turned up. Do you want him to play back now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I do not need to; the gentleman who was just talking, who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was General Zivota Panic. General Panic at the time of the operation around Vukovar was commander of the 1st military district of the JNA, the military district responsible for the operations in Eastern Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in the autumn, summer/autumn of 1991. Following that, from the beginning of 1992, from I think January 1992, General Panic became Chief of Staff of the JNA, replacing General Blagoje Adzic, the previous Chief of Staff. So he moved from being commander of the 1st military district to being Chief of the General Staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be continued on, please? Stopping for a moment, please. Who was that who just immediately appeared on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Vojislav Seselj who is leader of the Serbian Radical Party and also leader or was leader of the paramilitary Serbian Chetnik movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was a politician in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is a Member of Parliament in Belgrade. He is currently a Member of Parliament in Belgrade and was at the time, and was also leader and organiser of this paramilitary volunteer group which went to fight in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period where he is speaking now, what period is he referring to, or perhaps you would like to listen to it?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Actually when he was speaking, when was that, what time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The image on which we stopped was Seselj making a speech, I would estimate, in the first half of 1991, though I cannot tell you exactly. It might have been into the second half of 1991. I identified it as being this period because he speaks of the Ustasha, the Ustasha groups, who are threatening Serbian people in Croatia. You may recall, when we discussed the Second World War, I identified the Ustasha as the fascist group that was put in power in the independent state of Croatia. The term "Ustasha" was one which was being used quite a lot by the Serbian elements in 1990 and 1991 with reference to Croatian nationalists as a whole, although within that it was clear that some people who had been associated with Ustasha families were returning to Croatia in that period giving some element of support to the use of that term, but it was widely used in a more or less blanket way to refer to any Croatian nationalist movement. In this case, Seselj, by using the term "Ustasha" is using it to indicate, to mobilize, support among people in Serbia to go and help what he regards as being the Serbs in Croatia threatened by the Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the tape be continued, please? Just stopping there, can you tell us what he is referring to at that particular point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is referring to an incident which occurred at Borovo Selo, a village on the outskirts of Vukovar in May 1991. This was an incident in which, according to this, Seselj's paramilitaries, ambushed members of the Croatian Police Force resulting in an incident in which as far as I recall I think it was 12 members of the Croatian Police Force were injured, sorry, were killed and a further number were injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be played on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would also point out ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just stopping there again, that is Seselj again, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Seselj wearing a combat outfit and a helmet, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was generally regarded as head of a particular paramilitary group, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was regarded as being the leader of the Serbian Chetnik movement. His name has also sometimes been associated with a group known as White Eagles, although that group was, as far as I could see, formerly led by Mirko Jovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That period of time, what would the date have been on that, the first time 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say the date on that would be November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If the tape could be continued, please. Just stopping there for a moment, please. Now who is the gentleman that we see on the screen there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This gentleman is Dragoslav Bokan who again was leader of one of the small paramilitary groups. The previous extract we saw with the men in uniform shouting was a scene of the Serbian volunteer guard, that is the so-called Tigers organised by Zeljko Raznjatovic known as Arkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the previous segment where Seselj was speaking he made references I think a couple of times to the regime in Serbia. Are you able to assist us in what he was referring to there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seselj was indicating that his paramilitary group was receiving assistance from official bodies of the Republic of Serbia but in terms of being given barracks and facilities and in terms of being given equipment of various types, including arms, to go and be active. I am not sure if he is making reference to a particular period. I would say he is making reference generally to the period from spring 1991, certainly from the second half of 1991 onwards and refers both to Croatia and to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When you say "onwards" do you mean after May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say after May 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it could be continued on, please. Just stopping there for a moment. Do you know, are you able to assist us again in a time frame when he said, "We were just told to go to one place or the other"? Do you know what time frame he is talking about or can you suggest it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would suggest that he is talking about the whole time frame for the period after May 1991 continuing into and through 1992 and quite probably beyond that. I would also point out, which does not appear in the translation, that he also makes reference to Vladmir Bogdanovic who was head of the Serbian Security Service and that Bogdanovic was one of the people who spoke to him in making these arrangements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it could be played on thank you. Thank you. Dr. Gow, who was Michail ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What time frame do you think he is talking about when he said that "Serbia asked me to send my fighters"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he would be talking he or could be talking about any part of the time frame after May 1991. In the particular extract you just saw he was making particular reference to giving assistance to the Bosnian Serbs. I would assume that that would be in the course of 1992 and possibly in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you move on to another part or to another area of questioning, we are going to take a recess for until 4.30. (4.10 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Before you begin, I wonder if I can clarify one bit of the evidence we have already heard, and that is these percentages we have had of Serbs in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: When the witness speaks of Serbs, is he talking of citizens or inhabitants of Serbia, or is he talking of people who may be citizens of Croatia but of Serb orientation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Yes, Dr. Gow, could you assist us with the matter that was raised by His Honour in relation to the Serbs you referred to in your various charts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gladly. Although the ethnic key system which was intended to provide a degree of proportionality, I made reference to this, I noted Article 242 of the Constitution, specifically looked for equal representation by republics and provinces. When I used the term "Serbs" I was using it by the designation of those who would regard themselves by an ethno-national label, for want of a better term, as Serbs rather than as citizens of Serbia. So they would be Serbs, could quite probably be Serbs from Croatia or from Bosnia rather than Serbs from Serbia itself or non, people not ethnically Serb from Serbia. It refers to the ethnic identification and the process of self-identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I take it you have no statistics which would identify numbers in the JNA at any particular time who are citizens of Serbia or citizens of the new entity formed by Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have figures for citizens of Serbia. The figures which indicate, which I gave to indicate for March 1992, the reports of the ethnic composition, I would say made reference to people who were citizens of Serbia and Montenegro and who defined themselves as Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, who was Mihalj Kertes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mihalj Kertes was the Deputy Federal Interior Minister and was reported as being head of the Federal Security Service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did he play in the establishment of the paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It appears that Kertes and the Head of the Serbian Security Service, Radmilo Bogdanovic to whom I made reference before the recess, were instrumental in helping to organise and establish the paramilitary groups according to reports and Serbian sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you look at the document that I now show to you, please. (Handed). Dr. Gow, what is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a transcript, I am sorry, not a transcript, the text of the intervention of Mr. Ivan Panic who at the time in question, the time this document was prepared, was Prime Minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is Serbia and Montenegro. The document is Intervention at the London Conference of August 1992. The London conference was a major international conference jointly sponsored by the United Nations and by the European Union and under the presidency of the European Union of the United Kingdom. It took place between August 26th and 28th 1992, and involved representatives of all the European Union countries, of the Security Council countries and of a number of other international representatives, and gave rise to the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia which was to sit in Geneva after September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the document came from in terms of the copy you have there, do you know who obtained it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The copy, this copy, was obtained by me from the London conference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I gather that is Exhibit 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once the document has been marked might it be returned to the witness. Now, perhaps going to page 3 in particular, firstly, would you have a look at page 3 and, in relation to that, could you tell us the significance of what appears there? Just put it on the overhead projector, page 3 and page 4 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the text of this intervention Mr. Panic, who was of Serbian Yugoslav origin who emigrated in the 1950s to the United States and was and is an American citizen, was at the time he became Prime Minister of Serbia and Montenegro, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in making this intervention he was trying to represent Yugoslavia and to promote a policy of peace and indicated, as here, that his government, according to his statement, firmly and categorically opposed any use of force to change borders between countries and accepted the borders drawn between the republics of the SFRY as the official international borders between Yugoslavia and its neighbouring countries, and confirmed that they had no claims on those neighbouring countries, and at the same time that his government had already moved to recognise the republic of Slovenia and its independent international personality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic indicates the categoric rejection of what he describes as the barbaric practice of ethnic cleansing in any form, and goes on to say that he will try to bring to justice any Yugoslav citizen, that is a citizen of Serbia and Montenegro, against whom evidence could be obtained of having engaged in any act of ethnic cleansing, and goes on to say that in town Hrtkovci Vojvodina he had in fact arrested, had caused to have arrested the Mayor in the previous week for involvement in practices associated with ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might the Exhibit be returned to the Registry. I am sorry, do you wish to refer to another part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may move on to the insert on page 4 which I regard as being the significant part, or the most significant part, of this document is that until the first paragraph, and this was a late insertion in the Intervention, Mr. Panic points out that he had cause to be dismissed I think on that very morning one of his Deputy Interior Ministers, that is the man to whom I made reference before, Mihalj Kertes, and the reason he gives for that dismissal is Kertes' opposition to the policy of opposing ethnic cleansing. I will just indicate here, "I will fire any", "One of my Vice Ministers failed to support my government policy of firm active opposition to ethnic cleansing. I fired him this morning. I will fire any other Federal government official employee who, by actions or inactions, supports ethnic cleansing in any form whatsoever." In drawing this to your Honours' attention I think it would also be appropriate to point out that Mr. Panic is an American citizen, had been brought in and was Prime Minister for temporary period, that his Prime Minister-ship is usually seen as being an attempt by Serbia and Montenegro, particularly by Serbia, let us say, to try to present a more amenable image to the world, and that Mr. Panic, whilst he was trying to take Yugoslavia in one direction, had relatively little real power and a demonstration of this was that in the following October, this was in August 1992, in the following October forces of the Serbian Interior Ministry occupied the Federal Interior Ministry and allowed Mr. Kertes to return to his desk in the Interior Ministry building there and take up his activities in sitting in the office of a Deputy Federal Interior Minister and, presumably, continuing to run the Federal Security Service, if the reports that that is what he did are accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the JNA at any stage become involved in distribution of military supplies to the paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did. The JNA was involved in allowing access to arms, first of all, in the Knin area in Croatia to local Serbian forces, according to widespread political reports, and was later to play a significant role in distributing arms to Serbian irregular forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow, now turning to what is described as the new political project ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When would this have been, Dr. Gow? When, the date? When would the JNA have either distributed supplies to paramilitary groups or allowing access to supplies in Knin, when, what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The access to arms in the Knin area would have been in the latter part of 1990. The distribution of weaponry and other materials to irregular forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina would have been in the latter part of 1991 and through the first months of 1992, until the point at which the JNA ceased to exist in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow, turning to the new political project, what was the reaction of the JNA to the declarations of independence by Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA rejected the declarations of independence by Slovenia and Croatia and deployed troops in response to those declarations of independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the documents which you are now shown. (Handed). Can you tell me what the document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is an extract from an English language publication published in Ljubija, the capital of Slovenia, in August 1991 and is titled "War in Slovenia" and contains extracts from relevant documentation for that period translated into English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour, and it is No. 39. .

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Exhibit 39?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 39 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a translation of an instruction given by the Federal Government on 21st June 1991 instructing the Ministry of Defence to co-operate with the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs in implementing and enforcing the border points of the SFRY with Italy, Austria and Hungary, that is in the event of a declaration of independence by the Republic of Slovenia. This was the basis on which after the declarations of independence on 25th June 1991 the forces of the JNA were deployed in Slovenia with the mission of securing the international border crossing points between what was and had been the border of the SFRY in Slovenia with the neighbouring countries. It was of limited deployment, it was of limited assistance to civil authorities to assist the Interior Ministry in taking and ensuring federal control of border posts. This was of course opposed by the Republic of Slovenia, and was later the Federal Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, was later to point out that the JNA and its activities had gone beyond the instructions, the orders given in this federal government document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. If that exhibit could be returned. Would you look for me, please, at document No. 40, the one I show you now. (Handed). What is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an extract taken from the Volume Yugoslavia Through Documents edited by Snezana Trifunovska to which we have made reference already, and this particular extract is a document "Stands and Conclusions of the SFRY Presidency" concerning the situation in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where is it obtained? What is its source, can you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the present form it is obtained from the Trifunovska volume which I just mentioned. Trifunovska obtained it from their review of International Affairs published in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 40. Any objection? What is the date on that, I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 27th June 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection? None. Exhibit 40 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think paragraph 3 on page 306 of the document; it is really the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 of this Stands and Conclusions of the SFRY Presidency supports the decision of the Federal Government. The reference to the Federal Executive Council you see here is what I have been describing as the Federal Government. This is a statement of the presidency supporting the decision of the Federal Executive Council to attempt to ensure respect for the crossing, for the state frontier crossing points between Slovenia, on the territory of the Republic of Slovenia, and prohibiting the setting up of any other new frontier crossing points. It also, if you look to the final sentence of that paragraph, expresses approval for the participation of the Yugoslav People's Army in particular this these activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the reaction of the international community to the JNA intervention in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I might point out one more thing about this document, if you permit me, before I go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is, at this stage because of the declarations of independence by Slovenia and Croatia, the SFRY presidency was no longer in any sense the SFRY presidency as had been but was a rump presidency without participation from those republics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps the Exhibit might be marked. Dr. Gow, what was the reaction of the international community to the JNA intervention in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a marked international response, particularly this response was focused in the reaction of the European Council of European Communities. The European I refer to for convenience as the "European Community". The EC immediately decided, among other things, to dispatch its presidential troika to seek to mediate in the conflict on the territories of the SFRY. The presidential troika, for clarification, comprises the President, the current President of the European Community or European Union, the present and the President in waiting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just looking at this document that is now shown to you, is this a reference to the reaction taken by the European Community? Can you tell us what the document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is again an extract taken from the Trifunovska volume, Yugoslavia through Documents, and contains two elements. The first element is a short statement by the European Community and its Member States, showing alarm at the hostilities which had taken place, and it is dated 2 July 1991, this is after the ministerial troika of the European Community had begun its mission, and it also has the beginning of a second element in which the Committee of Senior Officials of CSC as it was then indicates its full support for the European Community. It indicates its concern and I think if we had the whole of it, it would go on to indicate its supports for the European Community mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that Exhibit, your Honour. That is No. 41. .

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 41?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 41 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might refer very quickly to the reference, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here at the top you have the short statement of concern by the European Community to which I made reference, dated 2 July 1991, and makes reference to the intervention of the ministerial troika of the European Community and its Member States which had already taken place and which was believed to have negotiated a cease-fire. The bottom part of that, I made reference to the Committee of Senior Officials of the CSC and its statement again regarding the situation on the territories of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps that Exhibit could be marked and returned. Dr. Gow, I would now like you to look at part 3, the video part 3, as it appears on your screen of Exhibit 31. Before you do, perhaps with relation to the exhibit list that has been distributed around the courtroom, if you could just put it on the screen and just show us the part that you were going to be shown on that list to assist?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Not to get back into that back, I do not think we have a problem with that, but there is just one part 3, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the section we will be seeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will ask that part 3 of Exhibit 31 be played. (Part 3 of Exhibit 31 was played). If you could just tell us what that short clip related to, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The clip showed Milan Kucan who at the time and indeed still is President of the Republic of Slovenia and Slobodan Milosevic at the time and presently President of the Republic of Serbia. The nature of the clip indicated a discussion which had taken place between those two Presidents of which there are two significant features. One is that the two of them had an understanding of the situation and that Milosevic was prepared to make some kind of a deal in which he would agree to Slovenian independence in exchange for Slovenian agreement to a change of the SFRY constitution. The second element is that it is clear from this that Milosevic was seeking to change the SFRY constitution to extend or to change the interpretation of sovereignty to apply to the nations, the peoples, that is what he would regard as ethno-national groups irrespective of their territorial boundaries. This is of significance for what is to come afterwards, I believe, because the argument between the Yugoslav republics had been on the basis of the constitutional divisions of 1974 and the sovereignty of the republics. Those arguments were carried forward into talks and into a conference with the European Community about the sovereignty of the republics. The second aspect of this that I am highlighting indicates the degree to which the Serbian President recognised the existing constitutional provisions and the need to change them if the Serbian people as a whole, that is the Serbian people not only within Serbia but within Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia as well, were to be included, were to be given the right to self-determination under these provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Do you mean that Milosevic was not talking sarcastically then? Does he not say not only give it to the nations but to every minority group? I had thought sarcastic but I must be wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall he does not say that. I believe he was seriously arguing that there should be a change. The Republic of Serbia at the European Community conference in the autumn of 1991 was to put forward the question as to whether or not the Serbs in Croatia were entitled, had the right to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would your Honours like to see the clip again or is that sufficient? .

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you ask us, yes, we do. Particularly in the light of Judge Stephen's question I would like to see it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could it be replayed, please? (The video clip was replayed). Dr. Gow, is it fair to say that at that particular time Serbia did not have the same interests in Slovenia, the Republic of Serbia did not have interests in Slovenia in the same way as it may have had in other parts of Yugoslavia where there were Serb minorities or Serb populations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true to say that there was not a significant Serbian population in the Republic of Slovenia and, therefore, Serbia had less reason or opportunity to support or to oppose Slovenian independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I was going to ask for an exhibit to be returned but it may be being copied. If that is the case I will not go to it. I was looking for Exhibit 30 but if it is outside I can move on and I will. I would ask you to look at this next document that I show you. (Handed). What is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a copy of an article written in the journal Foreign Affairs in July/August 1994 written by David Gompert. Gompert was formally Senior Director for Europe and Eurasia of the National Security Council of the US administration under President Bush.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 42 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If the document could be handed back to the witness. Dr. Gow, I think there is a footnote that you might take us to on the third page of the Exhibit which is 36 of the article. Perhaps just that footnote could be highlighted. There will need to be a lot of highlighting I think.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The article is called "How to Defeat Serbia", is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is it, your Honour. What is the significance of this footnote, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my interpretation the JNA when it originally deployed in Slovenia in response to the declaration of independence and in accordance with the instruction of the Federal Government dated 21 June 1991, to which I already made reference, it was not attempting to go to war in Slovenia; it was attempting to enforce the then federal regulations as interpreted by the Federal Government and became engaged in an armed conflict with Slovenian territorial defences forces. In part it was doing this because it assumed that either the Slovenes would not fight and respond or that if they were to fight and respond that it would to be able to escalate its activities and take control of Slovenia. In my judgment, the intervention of the international community, particularly under the auspices of the European Community, changed that perspective. If you recall from one of the video clips we saw before, Borisav Jovic was indicating that in March Kadijevic had already been worried about a western response to any action by the JNA. I believe that by the time of the declarations of independence the JNA Generals had felt assured that there would be no external intervention, but the then intervention by the European Community changed its perspective. All of this is my interpretation of the events. In that context I think the JNA was later to begin to become very worried following on from the EC intervention, following on from other discussions in the international community about the prospect of some kind of western intervention, bearing in mind that the Gulf conflict of 1990/91 was still fresh in minds. In this context I cite Gompert as senior official of the US Administration indicating that after the Rome Summit of the North Atlantic treaty organisation NATO in November 1991, General Kadijevic had indicated to him the belief that the alliance was preparing a force to intervene on the territories of former Yugoslavia against the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, moving from Slovenia into Croatia, how did the JNA conduct the war against Croatia in the second half of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already discussed the way in which the JNA originally deployed troops out of barracks in Croatia with the purpose, ostensibly, of preventing intercommunal conflict, it is sometimes called peacekeeping, but how, according to General Kadijevic, that was really de facto a mechanism for giving assistance to and helping to protect in its terms Serbs in Croatia. As Yugoslavia moved into this final phase of dissolution following the declarations of independence, General Kadijevic and others have identified that the JNA had two phases of objectives for the campaign in Croatia, both involving the utilization of Serbian populations and of irregulars and paramilitary groups. The first phase would be to secure those territories in which there was majority or significant Serbian populations and, as far as possible, to join those areas. The second phase would then be to move on and to defeat Croatia as a whole and to try to topple the Croatia government of Franjo Tudjman. The record, the historical record shows that the JNA was unable to move to that second phase and also, according to both General Kadijevic and General Panic in their writings, it was unable even to achieve completely its aims within the first phase of operations, that is to secure the territories around majority Serbian populations or adjacent to those populations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with the war against Croatia, would you look at the document I now show you?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask just one question? What is the import of this exhibit, Exhibit 42, footnote 1? I am just asking. Maybe I should not ask you. Maybe I should ask Mr. Niemann. Are you asking us to look at footnote 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this the article "How to Defeat Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The significance is in my terms, in terms of the evidence that I am trying to give presenting the JNA position during the war in Croatia, is to indicate the concern which the senior generals in the JNA had about the prospect of western military intervention, as the other side of the evidence that I gave earlier to indicate that, although they were talking about the rubric of separating communities, preventing intercommunal strife, in fact this was a guise for another of kind of activity which was the campaign to create the borders of the new entity, the new Yugoslavia, embracing parts of Croatia and later to be embracing parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The reason for showing this is to indicate the concern about a western military intervention. It is that concern about a western military intervention which led the JNA to continue not to declare explicitly what it was trying to do, but to conduct the campaign to create the new the borders of the new entity without openly saying that that is what it was trying to do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you look at this document, the one you are now shown. (Handed). Dr. Gow, clearly that is a map. What is it a map of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a map of the territories of the former Yugoslavia on which are indicated the zones of Serbian control within Croatia and the main axes of JNA operations in phase one of operations in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that map, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 43?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Objection to 42, did I ask you whether you have an objection to 42?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You did not, but no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I did not think so. Fine. Then Exhibit 42 is admitted and Exhibit 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, just looking at the exhibit that is now displayed on the screen, can you trace for us, please, the progress of the war against Croatia in the second half of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this map you will see indicated two shaded areas on here, one here and the other there. This is the area broadly known as Krajina, including the areas moving through the Banija and Kordun to western Slavonia here. This is the area of Eastern Slavonia. These were areas some of which had majority Serbian populations, some of which had significant Serbian populations and areas in which Serbian forces in conjunction with the JNA took control in the course of 1991. You also see some red, some lines with arrows indicated moving from Gradiska to Virovitica, from Bihac to Karlovac, from Knin to Zadar on the coast and from Mostar in western Herzegovina, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, through to Split on the coast. The lines from Banja Luka here indicate that it was from the forces from the Banja Luka Corps which were engaged in the operations identified here moving toward Karlovac and towards Virovitica. Those axes, those lines of attack and operations, are the ones identified by General Kadijevic in his book for this phase of the war in Croatia. I would also add that in broad terms if somebody was wanting to try to identify the borders which were being sought to be established in this phase of the conflict, then you would probably draw the line from Veravititsa, through Karlovac down to Zadar and down to Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might that document be returned to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I just may, I forgot to point out there was one small area on the southern Dalmatian coast under Serbian control at that time as well, sorry, under JNA control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might that be returned to the Registrar. I would now ask that part 4 of Exhibit 31 be played. Perhaps if it just be played through first and then I will ask you to discuss it following that, please, Dr. Gow. (Part 4 of Exhibit 31 was played). Now just stopping there for a moment, can you tell us the time frame of that clip, what it relates to, what period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Admiral Branko Mamula that we made reference to and we saw him on the video clip earlier, and he was making reference to this period of the war in Croatia in the second half of 1991. What he was specifically making reference to was what would be identified as phase two of operations as expressed by General Kadijevic in his book and the intention through a two-pronged attack, once the first phase had been established for a two-pronged attack to move on Zagreb and topple the Croatian regime. This was part of the programme which was never accomplished. As far as I can see, they never actually moved to try to implement phase two. The reason for that was the lack of support among Serbian communities to move further at that stage and a lack of manpower resources within the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just play it again quickly, thank you. Dr. Gow, with respect to the war in southern Croatia, did the JNA act alone or did it have the assistance of paramilitary forces? I am referring particularly to southern Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were on the map that I indicated before, I showed the areas of Serbian control and, indeed, of the Serbian JNA operation, each of those areas had a distinct characteristic. The area of Eastern Slovenia involved JNA forces operating in conjunction with the paramilitary groups coming from Serbia itself and some local forces, but primarily from Serbia itself. The largest area indicated involved the JNA and some paramilitary groups from Serbia itself some of the time, but primarily local Serbs, and the final area, the area in Southern Dalmatia, the area leading up the Konavle district to Dubrovnik, was an operation which was conducted almost entirely by the JNA itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps it might assist ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some small part paramilitary ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: --- if you could point to it on Exhibit 43?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gladly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps Exhibit 43 could be shown. Could you point to the area in Dalmatia where the JNA was operating.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. You see I indicated, I mentioned the three areas, Eastern Slovenia where the JNA was operating primarily with paramilitary groups from Serbia itself, the larger area here in which the JNA was giving assistance primarily to local Serbs, and the area down here, the strip of coast, the coastal area down here leading up to the town of Dubrovnik which is about there somewhere, which was notable for the siege of Dubrovnik in the autumn of 1991, in that area the JNA was acting more or less alone, operations out of Montenegro and out of Trebinje in Herzegovina, in this part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, moving to occupy that coastal strip.
